body:
Hi,
this error usually happens when Next.js is not properly installed or not resolved in the project, especially when using Turbopack.

The message
Next.js package not found
often means that the next dependency is missing, corrupted, or the install failed.

Things you can try:

Make sure next is listed in your package.json dependencies

Reinstall dependencies:

rm -rf node_modules pnpm-lock.yaml
pnpm install


Verify Next.js is installed:

pnpm list next


As Turbopack is still experimental, try running without it:

next dev --no-turbo


If you are on Windows, also make sure symlinks are allowed (Developer Mode enabled or run terminal as Administrator), since pnpm + Turbopack relies on them.

This seems more like an environment / dependency resolution issue rather than an app code issue.

Hope this helps 👍

body:
Hi,
this looks like a Turbopack internal state / cache issue rather than a problem with the application code itself.

The error
Cell ... AppPageLoaderTree no longer exists in task directory_tree_to_loader_tree
suggests that Turbopack’s internal task graph became invalid, which can happen during HMR or after file structure changes in the app/ directory.

Things you can try:

Stop the dev server and clear build caches:

rm -rf .next node_modules
pnpm install
pnpm dev


Make sure your app/ directory structure is valid (e.g. app/page.tsx exists and there are no partially renamed or deleted files).

Restart the dev server after any file or folder rename inside app/.

Since Turbopack is still experimental, try disabling it:

next dev --no-turbo


If the issue only happens with Turbopack enabled, this may be a Turbopack bug rather than a Next.js configuration issue.

Hope this helps, and thanks for the great work on Next.js 👍

body:
Hi,
this looks like a Windows permission issue, not a problem with Next.js or Turbopack itself.

The error
os error 1314 (The client does not have a required privilege)
usually happens when Windows blocks the creation of symbolic links, which are used by pnpm.

Possible fixes:

Run your terminal or VS Code as Administrator

Enable Developer Mode in Windows (Settings → Privacy & Security → For developers)

Or configure pnpm to avoid symlinks:

pnpm config set node-linker=hoisted


As a workaround, you can also try running Next.js without Turbopack:

next dev --no-turbo


Hope this helps 👍

body:
this is a file descriptor limit issue - basically docker is running out of available file handles
try these things:

increase the file descriptor limit in your dockerfile by adding RUN ulimit -n 65536 before your CMD
or run the container with --ulimit nofile=65536:65536
try adding turbopack: { logLevel: 'error' } to your next config to reduce file watchers
you might also want to add .next to your .dockerignore if its not already there

the sentry setup might be watching too many files which is hitting the default limit. docker containers have much lower default limits than your local machine which is why it works locally but not in docker
also since it broke even after reverting changes you might have some corrupted cache somewhere. try doing a completely clean rebuild without cache using docker build --no-cache

body:
Hey @randyliugogoout — I ran into a very similar issue a while back and spent quite some time debugging it, so hopefully this helps.

## What's happening

The root cause is a race condition between **streaming** and **Googlebot's rendering budget**. When Next.js streams an ISR page, the initial HTML shell is sent first with an empty `<title>` placeholder, and the actual metadata is delivered later via the RSC payload (`self.__next_f.push()`). The browser (or a full Chrome renderer) will execute that JS and patch the `<title>` in — but Googlebot doesn't always wait long enough for that to happen.

This is especially problematic with ISR because during **revalidation windows**, the stale page might be served while Next.js regenerates in the background. If Googlebot hits the page at exactly that moment, the streamed response can have a timing gap where the metadata hasn't resolved yet.

## Why it's random 

Google's crawler has a [two-phase indexing process](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics#how-googlebot-processes-javascript):

1. **First wave** — crawls raw HTML (no JS execution)
2. **Second wave** — renders with a headless Chromium (WRS - Web Rendering Service)

If Googlebot indexes during the first wave and the `<title>` is empty in the initial HTML chunk, it records an empty title. The second wave *usually* fixes this, but not always — Google's rendering queue can have significant delays, and sometimes the first-wave result sticks.

## Practical fixes

**Option 1: Force static generation with `generateStaticParams`**

If your routes are known at build time, make sure they're fully pre-rendered so the HTML already contains the complete `<title>`:

```ts
// app/[lang]/suggestion/city/[slug]/page.tsx
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  return [
    { lang: 'zh-tw', slug: 'taitung-car-rental' },
    // ... other routes
  ];
}
```

This way the HTML is fully baked at build time — no streaming, no race condition.

**Option 2: Use a `<title>` tag directly in your root layout as a fallback**

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        {/* fallback title — generateMetadata will override this */}
        <title>Your Site Name</title>
      </head>
      <body>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

This ensures that even if the streamed metadata hasn't arrived yet, there's always *something* in the `<title>` tag. Not ideal, but prevents the empty-title problem for SEO.

**Option 3: Upgrade to Next.js 15+**

The streaming metadata behavior was significantly improved in Next.js 15. Specifically, [PR #64961](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/64961) addressed the metadata resolution timing during streaming. If upgrading from 14.2.x is feasible for your project, this alone might fix the issue.

## Verifying the fix

You can check what Googlebot actually sees by using:

- **Google Search Console → URL Inspection → "Test Live URL"** → click "View Tested Page" → check the HTML tab
- `curl -A "Googlebot" https://your-url` to see the raw initial HTML

If `<title>` is populated in the raw HTML response (before any JS), you're good.

Hope this helps — SEO issues from streaming are genuinely frustrating to debug. Let me know if you have questions.

body:
yeah so the issue is that unauthorized() works like an error boundary - it throws an error to show your unauthorized page. when you call router.refresh() from inside that error boundary, it just refreshes within that error state rather than escaping it.

inside handleSuccess you can either use `router.push('/');`, `window.location.href = '/';` or even better aproach to - use a server action with redirect
author: Tiimie1

body: `use a server action with redirect `also unable to work
author: Scholar01

body:
yeah you nailed it, `unauthorized()` throws into an error boundary, so `router.refresh()` just refreshes inside that boundary. it can't escape it.

`router.push('/')` has the same problem since it's still a client-side navigation within the error boundary.

the only way out is a hard navigation:

```ts
window.location.href = '/';  
```

it breaks out of React entirely and does a full server roundtrip, so auth gets re-evaluated fresh. not the most elegant but it's the correct approach here since you need to escape the error boundary.

body:
I understand this means symlinks/junctions cannot be created on a filesystem that is part of a bind mount of volume inside Docker. I'm not sure if this is a limitation of Docker or Windows Containers, but it is a known limitation, and basically the only way around it is not to bind a Docker container to the app root, which creates the challenge of having to create lots of fine-grained mounts, leaving the `.next` directory internal to the container. This is not a sustainable solution.

The other solution is something I can't control (but you can!) - just don't use symlinks/junctions if the OS or FS reports an error when trying them.

I believe similar errors will be thrown when working off a different type of storage that also doesn't support symlinks/junctions, like maybe a network drive, or an exFAT/FAT32 drive (like an external disk). Or indeed a mounted directory in a Windows container.

I'd be interested to know what you choose to be the solution.

body:
This green tint issue with AVIF images in production is a **libvips color profile handling bug** that affects specific sharp/libvips version combinations on certain platforms.

## Root Cause

The issue stems from:
1. **libvips color space conversion** - When sharp (which uses libvips) converts AVIF images, it may incorrectly handle ICC color profiles
2. **Platform-specific binaries** - Your AWS production environment has different libvips binaries than your local machine
3. **Missing or incompatible libheif** - The AVIF decoder (libheif) version in production may not match the one locally

## Solutions

### Solution 1: Pin Sharp Version (Recommended)

Downgrade to a known-working sharp version:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "sharp": "0.33.5"
  },
  "overrides": {
    "sharp": "0.33.5"
  }
}
```

Then:
```bash
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
```

### Solution 2: Force Rebuild Sharp in Production

Ensure sharp uses platform-specific binaries:

**Option A - Using npm scripts:**
```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "npm rebuild sharp && next build"
  }
}
```

**Option B - In your Dockerfile (if using Docker):**
```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine

# Install libvips dependencies
RUN apk add --no-cache \
    libvips-dev \
    build-base \
    python3

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
RUN npm rebuild sharp

COPY . .
RUN npm run build
```

### Solution 3: Disable AVIF in next.config.js

Temporary workaround - use WebP instead:

```javascript
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
module.exports = {
  images: {
    formats: ['image/webp'], // Remove AVIF
  },
};
```

### Solution 4: Force Specific Sharp Config

Create a custom image loader that handles color spaces explicitly:

```javascript
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  images: {
    loader: 'custom',
    loaderFile: './imageLoader.js',
  },
};
```

```javascript
// imageLoader.js
export default function imageLoader({ src, width, quality }) {
  return `/_next/image?url=${encodeURIComponent(src)}&w=${width}&q=${quality || 75}`;
}
```

### Solution 5: Update Environment Variables

Set these in your AWS deployment:

```bash
SHARP_IGNORE_GLOBAL_LIBVIPS=1
SHARP_FORCE_GLOBAL_LIBVIPS=0
```

This forces sharp to use its bundled libvips rather than system-installed versions.

## Best Practice Fix

**For AWS Lambda/Serverless:**
```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "sharp": "0.33.5"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@img/sharp-linux-x64": "0.33.5"
  }
}
```

**For AWS EC2/ECS:**
Add this to your build process:
```bash
npm install --platform=linux --arch=x64 sharp
```

## Why This Happens

Next.js 16.1.1 updated its image optimization dependencies, which changed how sharp/libvips handles AVIF color spaces. The green tint specifically indicates **YUV to RGB conversion issues** where the chroma channels are misinterpreted.

## Debugging Steps

1. Check sharp version in production:
```bash
node -e "console.log(require('sharp').versions)"
```

2. Compare local vs production:
```bash
# Local
node -e "console.log(process.platform, process.arch)"

# Should match your production environment
```

## Related Issues

- [Next.js Issue #58601](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/58601)
- [Sharp Issue #3750](https://github.com/lovell/sharp/issues/3750)

The Next.js team is aware of this and working on better cross-platform compatibility for image optimization.

body: In the Next.js App Router, a catch-all segment like: `app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/route.ts` must be the last path segment. You cannot put anything “under” it, like: `app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/create/route.ts` # or `app/api/auth/[...nextauth]/create.ts` That’s exactly what Turbopack is complaining about: it found segments like `/api/auth/[...nextauth]/create → catch-all is not last.` I will recommend make `create` a sibling route Move `create` out from under `[...nextauth]:` `app/ api/ auth/ [...nextauth]/ route.ts create/ route.ts ` Now your routes are - 1. POST /api/auth/* handled by NextAuth catch-all 2. POST /api/auth/create handled by your custom route

body:
this usually happens when the .next folder has wrong permissions or is owned by a different user.

try these fixes:

1. delete .next folder and rebuild:
```bash
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
```

2. if that doesnt work, check ownership:
```bash
ls -la .next
```

if its owned by root or different user:
```bash
sudo chown -R $(whoami):$(whoami) .
```

3. if running in docker or as different user previously, the files might be locked:
```bash
sudo rm -rf .next
mkdir .next
```

4. check if any process is holding files:
```bash
lsof +D .next/
# kill any processes if needed
```

5. if using turbopack with file watching, the watch process might have stale handles:
```bash
killall node
npm run dev
```

6. check disk space:
```bash
df -h .
```

7. if problem persists, try disabling turbopack temporarily:
```bash
npm run dev -- --turbopack=false
```

the os error 13 is linux permission denied error, so its definitely a filesystem permission issue, not turbopack itself.

body:
400 malformed request from server actions usually means:

1. **csrf token mismatch** - check if cookies are being blocked or expired

2. **request body too large** - check if youre sending large files

3. **content-type header issue**

debug steps:

1. **check browser devtools network tab:**
- look at request headers
- check request payload
- is content-type correct?

2. **add logging to server action:**
```ts
"use server"
export async function myAction(formData: FormData) {
  console.log("action called", Object.fromEntries(formData))
}
```

3. **check if middleware is interfering:**
temporarily disable any custom middleware

4. **common causes:**
- adblocker blocking requests
- vpn/proxy modifying headers
- nextjs version mismatch between dev and prod
- serverless function size limit

5. **try clearing .next folder:**
```bash
rm -rf .next
npm run build
```

what next.js version are you on? and did anything change recently - deployment, package updates?

Apparently this mitigation was a bit too strict and denied valid requests as well. They updated their rules and now everything is working again.

body:
The issue you're facing isn’t actually an issue — it’s one of those “it’s not a bug, it’s a feature” situations.

It happens because the Cache component internally relies on React’s `<Activity>` to preserve component state during client-side navigation.
https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/cache-components#navigation-uses-activity

So when navigating on the client, the previous state is reused instead of resetting the component.

Related discussions:

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/89160  
- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/86577

body:
Chiming in with a related observation that may help narrow down the underlying issue.

We are seeing a very similar symptom in our app, but **without Cache Components enabled** (no `experimental.cacheComponents` / `useCache` in `next.config.js`).

### Setup

- Next.js **16.2.4** (App Router)
- React 19.2.5
- Apollo Client v4 (via `@apollo/experimental-nextjs-app-support` 0.14.x)
- `export const revalidate = 0` on the affected page
- `<Link prefetch={false}>` for in-page filter navigation
- Same dynamic route (`/store/staffsnap/[[...slug]]`), only `searchParams` change

### Symptom

Under slow network (~Slow 4G), when the user clicks `<Link>` to change `searchParams` (e.g. toggling multiple color filters in succession), the URL bar updates correctly but the Server Component's rendered output (breadcrumb, server-fetched product list) stays **one navigation behind**. A hard refresh restores consistency, confirming that the URL and client state are fine but the wrong RSC payload was committed.

### Isolation testing

We bisected this:

| Config | Apollo | Next.js | Symptom |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` (before upgrade) | v3 | 15 | ✗ not reproduced |
| Apollo v4 only | v4 | **15** | ✗ not reproduced |
| Current | v4 | **16** | ✓ reproduced (~30%) |

→ The race is **not caused by Apollo Client v4 cancel behavior**. It appears only after upgrading Next.js to 16 (with Apollo unchanged).

### Workaround we implemented

A small Client Component compares `useSearchParams().toString()` against the `searchParams` string the Server Component rendered with (passed down as a prop). When they diverge, it calls `router.refresh()` to force a fresh SSR. This works reliably and visibly mitigates the symptom for users, but it is clearly a band-aid — the root issue is that a stale RSC payload is committed last in a concurrent navigation sequence.

Happy to share a minimal reproduction repo if it would help. The bisection points more to the client router / RSC commit ordering side than to caching, which differs from this thread's Cache Components angle — but the user-visible symptom (URL correct, server-rendered tree one step behind) is the same. Posting in case the same root cause underlies both reports.
author: muji-junkanai

body:
This is a Next.js router cache issue, not a data cache or `'use cache'` issue, which is why removing caching directives had no effect.

**What is actually happening**

The Next.js client-side router caches RSC payloads keyed by URL. When you push `?q=foo`, the router fetches the RSC payload and caches it. When you later push `?q=bar` and then `?q=foo` again, the router serves the previously cached RSC payload for `?q=foo` rather than making a new server request. The URL updates correctly in the browser, but the server component receives the searchParams from the cached payload, which is why you see the mismatch.

This is separate from the data cache and is controlled by `staleTimes` in your Next.js config.

**Fix 1: Set dynamic staleTime to 0 (most reliable)**

In `next.config.ts`:

```typescript
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    staleTimes: {
      dynamic: 0,
    },
  },
}
```

This tells the router to never serve a cached RSC payload for dynamically navigated routes, forcing a fresh server request every time. This is the correct setting for search pages where every navigation must reflect current searchParams.

**Fix 2: Force a fresh fetch on the specific navigation**

If you do not want to change the global `staleTimes`, you can force revalidation on the specific push:

```typescript
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
import { startTransition } from 'react'

const router = useRouter()

const handleSearch = (query: string) => {
  startTransition(() => {
    router.push(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)
    router.refresh()
  })
}
```

Wrapping both calls in `startTransition` ensures they are batched as a single transition. Calling `router.refresh()` after `router.push()` outside of `startTransition` can race, which is likely why it did not work reliably for you.

**Fix 3: Use a URL that busts the cache**

If neither of the above fits your architecture, appending a cache-busting param forces a unique URL per request and bypasses the router cache entirely:

```typescript
router.push(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}&t=${Date.now()}`)
```

This is a workaround rather than a proper fix but is useful for ruling out the router cache as the cause during debugging.

**Why Cache Components being enabled is relevant**

With Cache Components enabled in Next.js 16, the router makes more aggressive assumptions about what can be served from cache. Pages without any `'use cache'` directive are still subject to the router cache. The `staleTimes.dynamic` value defaults to a non-zero window specifically to make navigations feel instant, but this trades off correctness for search-style pages where every unique URL must produce a fresh render.

Setting `staleTimes.dynamic: 0` is the documented solution for this case and will not affect your data cache or `'use cache'` behavior.
author: GitNimay

body:
Follow-up on our case: we tested @GitNimay's Fix 1 (`experimental.staleTimes.dynamic: 0`) in isolation, and it did **not** stop the race we are seeing.

### Test setup

- Branch based on the production target (Next.js 16.2.4 + Apollo Client v4)
- `experimental.staleTimes.dynamic: 0` added explicitly to `next.config.js`
- Our workaround (`router.refresh()` based reconciler) disabled
- Cache Components **not enabled**
- Multiple team members verified locally under Slow 4G with the same color-filter toggling pattern as the original bug report

### Result

The same race reproduces — URL is up to date, but the Server Component rendered output stays one navigation behind. `router.refresh()` (our workaround) still recovers it; the explicit `staleTimes.dynamic: 0` alone does not.

### Why this likely doesn't fit the router cache hypothesis

The official Next.js docs for [staleTimes](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes) state:

> The `dynamic` property is used when the page is neither statically generated nor fully prefetched (e.g. with `prefetch={true}`). **Default: 0 seconds (not cached)**

| Version | Changes |
| --- | --- |
| v15.0.0 | The `dynamic` `staleTimes` default changed from 30s to 0s. |

Our app uses `<Link prefetch={false}>` as the default in the affected page (custom Link wrapper), so navigations go through the `dynamic` path which is documented as **never cached by default**. Explicitly setting it to 0 should be a no-op, which matches our observation.

So the symptom does not look like "the router is replaying an older cached payload for a previously-visited URL." It looks more like "the router commits a still-in-flight, now-obsolete RSC payload last in a concurrent navigation sequence." The symptom characteristics also support this:

- It can repro on **new URLs** the user has never visited before (no cached entry could exist)
- It is probabilistic (~30%), not deterministic — a cache hit would be 100% deterministic
- It reproduces even with **slow (1–2s interval) operation**, not just rapid clicks, suggesting the BFF response time widens the commit window rather than a navigation-burst race
- A hard reload always restores consistency (consistent with a stale committed tree, but also with a cached one — does not differentiate)

Sharing in case it helps narrow down the root cause — happy to provide the minimal repro once it's ready.

body:
A few things I'd check:

* Are you reading `searchParams` directly in the page, or inside a cached child component somewhere down the tree?
* Does the issue disappear if `cacheComponents: false` is set temporarily?
* Are you using a standard `<Suspense>` boundary around the search results?

With Cache Components enabled, search params become part of the cache keying story. I've seen cases where search/filter pages behave unexpectedly if the boundary isn't re-keyed on search param changes, especially when navigating between previously visited queries.

The fact that the URL is correct but the server component receives an older value makes me suspicious of router/cache state rather than `router.push()` itself.

I've been documenting a lot of these Next.js 16 cache/searchParams edge cases while building a cache architecture guide:

https://www.skills.sh/mohamed-hossam1/nextjs-cache-architecture/nextjs-cache-architecture

Repo:
https://github.com/mohamed-hossam1/nextjs-skills

There are examples around search-param boundaries, Cache Components, and debugging stale values. If it helps, a ⭐ on the repo would be appreciated.

body:
this error usually happens when node process crashes during css processing. few things to check:

1. clear turbopack cache and node_modules:
```bash
rm -rf .next node_modules
npm install
npm run dev
```

2. check if you have postcss config issues. if using tailwind, make sure postcss.config.js is correct:
```js
module.exports = {
  plugins: {
    tailwindcss: {},
    autoprefixer: {},
  },
}
```

3. check node version. turbopack can have issues with very old or very new node versions:
```bash
node --version
# try node 18 or 20 lts
```

4. the "node process exited before we could connect" often means oom or crash. try increasing memory:
```bash
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=8192" npm run dev
```

5. check your globals.css for any syntax errors or imports that might be failing.

6. if using tailwind v4, make sure you have the right config format:
```css
/* globals.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
```

7. try disabling turbopack temporarily to see if its turbopack specific:
```bash
npm run dev -- --turbopack=false
# or in next 15+
npm run dev -- --no-turbo
```

8. check if you have any circular imports in your css files.

if none of these work, share your package.json and postcss.config.js for more specific help.

Hi, did you manage to make any progress here? 

One thing you can quickly try is to turn off image optimization and see what the memory profile looks like during with that, get some data and turn on image optimization again.

As pointed out in the other comment, tweaking `--max-old-space-size` is often necessary too, because Node needs extra memory to run, other than the memory allocated by your user code so-to-speak.

Rule of thumb (AI suggestion):

- container limit 1024Mi → try heap 512–768
- container limit 2048Mi → try heap 1024–1536

A couple of other things are, making sure that you don't hold onto data globally, like when for each request you maybe copy some data into a global store, but never release it. Sometimes there's some Node.js patterns that implicitly do this, and never release memory, but these are less likely.

As mentioned above too, `standalone` mode can help, because it creates a minimal server, that can eliminate certain dependencies.

Try with next/image, tweak `--max-old-space-size`, and then switch Node.js version if possible, then Next.js version too, it is not uncommon for Node.js or Next.js to have released patches for some edge case memory leaks.

body:
Hi! The `Module not found` error in Next.js, especially when the file physically exists, is usually caused by one of a few common issues. Let's troubleshoot step by step:

### 1. Case Sensitivity (Most Common on Vercel/Linux)
If you are developing on Windows/Mac but deploying to Vercel (Linux), file paths are case-sensitive. Double-check that the casing in your import matches the actual folder/file name exactly.

// ❌ Wrong (if folder is `components`)
import Component from '@/Components/MyComponent'

// ✅ Correct
import Component from '@/components/MyComponent'

### 2. Path Alias Configuration (`@/*`)
Ensure your `tsconfig.json` or `jsconfig.json` includes the path mapping for `@`. If this is missing, the `@` alias won't work.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": {
      "@/*": ["./*"]
    }
  }
}

After adding this, **restart the dev server**.

### 3. File Extension
Next.js automatically resolves `.js`, `.jsx`, `.ts`, and `.tsx`. Make sure you are importing without the extension (just the file name), and that the file has one of those valid extensions.

### 4. Try Relative Path (Debugging Test)
To isolate if the issue is with the alias or the file itself, temporarily use a relative path:
import Component from '../components/MyComponent'

If this works but `@/` doesn't, the issue is definitely in your `tsconfig.json` configuration (Step 2).

### 5. Clear Next.js Cache
Sometimes the build cache gets stuck. Try deleting the `.next` folder and running again:
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
# or
yarn dev

Hope this helps! If one of these steps resolves it, let me know and I'll update the solution for others.

body:
This is a Turbopack panic error that occurs during development. Here are several solutions to try:

## Quick Fixes

### 1. **Disable Turbopack temporarily**
Set the environment variable to use Webpack instead:
```bash
NEXT_DISABLE_TURBOPACK=1 yarn dev
```

### 2. **Clear all caches**
```bash
# Delete Next.js cache
rm -rf .next

# Delete node_modules and reinstall
rm -rf node_modules
yarn install

# Clear yarn cache
yarn cache clean
```

### 3. **Check for problematic dependencies**
Turbopack can panic when encountering certain package configurations. Try:
- Updating to the latest Next.js version: `yarn add next@latest`
- Checking if any dependencies have known issues with Turbopack

### 4. **Windows-specific fixes** (since your path shows Windows)
- Run your terminal as Administrator
- Temporarily disable antivirus software (it can interfere with file watching)
- Check if the project path is too long (Windows has a 260 character limit)

### 5. **Review the panic log**
The panic log at `C:\Users\chen\AppData\Local\Temp\next-panic-fd85e20ad67fbeb622d3a654118ddfa9.log` contains the actual error. You can:
- Open that file to see more details
- Share the contents here for more specific help

## Report the Bug
If none of these work, please click the "report this error" link in your error message to help the Next.js team fix this issue.

## Alternative
If you need to continue development immediately, use Webpack mode:
```bash
next dev --no-turbopack
```

Let me know if any of these solutions work for you!

Hi! You’re right on both points.

PageProps is currently generated inside a gitignored dev-only folder, so CI/typecheck fails unless the dev server has been run.
Also, because it’s global, it can collide in monorepos with multiple Next.js apps.
A more reliable approach would be:

Generate it into a tracked location (e.g. app/.next/types or app/types)
Version control it (or at least make it available during next build)
Scope it to each app instead of global so monorepos don’t conflict.
If the goal is only to improve typing, a practical workaround today is to:

run next dev once before CI, or
generate it during next build, or
define a local PageProps type per app (non‑global).
So yes — making it non‑global and generated in a repo‑tracked or build‑time path would solve both CI and monorepo issues.

body: This issue in Next.js v16.0.3 usually stems from production-only inconsistencies such as hydration mismatches, stale build artifacts, or static asset loading problems. When the page renders correctly on the first refresh but intermittently shows a blank screen on subsequent reloads, it often indicates that the client-side bundle is either failing to hydrate or not being served properly. To address this, clear the `.next/` folder before each build to avoid stale artifacts, verify that `_next/static/` assets are being served correctly by your hosting setup, and ensure that any browser-only code is wrapped in `useEffect` to prevent server-side rendering conflicts. Adding error boundaries around your main layout or `_app.tsx` can help surface silent failures, and testing locally with `next build && next start` will often reveal hydration warnings that do not appear in development. If the issue persists, disabling experimental features like the app directory or React Server Components temporarily can help isolate the root cause.

body: **Root Cause Analysis** Intermittent blank screens on hard refresh (no console errors, production only) is a classic chunk loading failure pattern. The most common causes: - Stale CDN/browser cache serving old JS chunk hashes after a new deployment - Webpack chunk splitting generating filenames that 404 after redeployment - Hydration mismatch silently killing the render - Race condition in a client-side `useEffect` wiping content before paint _Start with Fix 1 and Fix 2 together — they resolve 80% of this pattern._ Hope this technical breakdown resolves your issue! body:
Hey! 👋 I ran into the same issue before. This usually happens when Turbopack cannot resolve the project path, especially with the new Next.js app folder routing. Here's how to fix it:

1️⃣ Check your folder structure

Make sure your src/ folder is inside your project root, like this:

my-project/
├─ package.json
├─ next.config.js
├─ src/
│  └─ app/
│     └─ (innerwebsite)/
│        └─ login/
│           └─ page.jsx


The (innerwebsite) folder is fine — it’s a route group, but the path must be inside the project root.

2️⃣ Enable appDir in next.config.js
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: { appDir: true },
};

module.exports = nextConfig;

3️⃣ Clear caches

Sometimes Turbopack caches wrong paths:

rm -rf .next
rm -rf node_modules/.cache
npm run dev

4️⃣ Check file names and imports

File name must be exactly page.jsx (casing matters)

Use relative imports inside login/:

import LoginForm from './LoginForm';

5️⃣ Optional: Disable Turbopack temporarily

If it still fails:

next dev --turbo false


This forces Webpack instead of Turbopack and usually works immediately.

💡 After doing this, your HMR should work and the error will disappear.

body:
Hey, this is a known issue with `"use cache"` in dynamic routes. You're not alone - several people have run into this exact behavior.

The core problem is that when a `"use cache"` function runs at runtime (in a dynamic context), Next.js treats the cached data as "expired" rather than "stale" after the revalidate period. This means it blocks and regenerates synchronously instead of serving stale content while revalidating in the background.

There's an open issue tracking this: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/74882 - it describes the exact same behavior where dynamic routes don't get stale-while-revalidate semantics that static routes get.

A few things that might help as workarounds:

1. **Use `generateStaticParams`** with at least one entry (even if you don't want to pre-render everything). This signals to Next.js that the route should use ISR behavior. Other paths not in the array will still be generated on-demand but should then cache properly.

2. **Avoid wrapping the cached component with Suspense** (including `loading.tsx`) - there seems to be some interaction between suspense boundaries and the caching behavior that causes issues.

3. If your use case allows, **move the expensive work to a separate cached function** that doesn't depend on dynamic params, then compose it with the dynamic data.

Unfortunately there's no perfect solution right now. The expectation (and docs) suggest it should work the way you expect - stale data served while revalidating - but it doesn't in dynamic contexts. This seems to be on the team's radar though.

Hope this helps clarify what's going on!

body:
Thanks for the update @nishatislam04 

Both features can add extra work at compile / render time, and in dev that cost can be paid more often because files/components are frequently invalidated.

- cacheComponents: it changes how parts of caching/PPR/dynamic IO are handled. The official docs even note it may introduce additional latency vs serving pre-rendered content.

- reactCompiler: it’s a compile-time transform. If your project is already on the edge of “many modules / heavy transforms,” dev can feel slower. (It’s designed to help runtime perf; it’s not guaranteed to speed up dev iteration.)

Recommendation: keep both enabled for prod builds, but disable them for development:

```js
const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV === "development";

/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: !isDev,
  cacheComponents: !isDev,
};

export default nextConfig;
```

Your logs still show “first-hit per route” compilation — that part is expected

In App Router dev, each route (and what it imports) can trigger compilation the first time you hit it.


Run Webpack dev (comparison)

Next has a webpack dev option — if webpack is dramatically faster/slower, that tells us where to dig.

```bash
bun --bun next dev --webpack
```

React Compiler is a feature of React / Next.js.
bun is just a runtime, package manager, and task runner.

That means:

- bun itself does not run or manage the React Compiler.

- But if Next.js supports the React Compiler, bun does not interfere with it and works just fine.

In other words, React Compiler is enabled and executed by Next.js, and bun simply runs Next.js.

body: @tomarrohitt This happens because useTransition is not actually tracking the server action itself, but whether React commits a new UI update. In production, when aggressive caching like cacheComponents: true is enabled, Next.js may decide that no new client tree needs to be committed (or it gets stuck behind a cached/suspense boundary), so the transition never “finishes” even though the server action and revalidation succeed. In development this is masked because caching is looser and extra renders happen, but in production the stricter cache + router behavior can leave pending stuck true even after the backend work is done.

author: tomarrohitt

body: @tomarrohitt Yes this isn’t just a useTransition issue. In Next.js 16, there are known production-only edge cases when cacheComponents: true is enabled where Server Actions + revalidation don’t force a client tree commit, even though the mutation and revalidatePath succeed. This can leave the UI showing cached RSC output until a hard reload, and it happens even if you replace useTransition with manual loading state because the problem is the router/RSC cache not emitting a fresh payload, not the spinner logic. In short: revalidatePath invalidates caches but doesn’t guarantee an immediate client update under aggressive component caching. For real-time UI like carts, you either need to disable component caching for that data/route or adopt cache tagging and invalidate the tag that the cart read is cached under.

body:
@tomarrohitt 
Likely yes but only if you do it correctly. The root problem is that with cacheComponents: true, your cart read can remain satisfied by cached RSC output, so the client never gets a “new tree” to commit.

	•	Making the cart route truly dynamic / uncached (so it must refetch after the action) is the most straightforward fix for a cart. If the cart data is read on /cart, don’t let that segment be component-cached.

	•	Using cache tags also works if your cart read is actually tagged and the action invalidates that same tag. If you tag the wrong place (or don’t tag the server read), nothing changes.

If you want a reliable cart UX, the “dynamic/uncached cart segment” approach is usually the safer choice; cache tags are fine, but easier to miswire.

body:
For anyone else pulling their hair out over this, it turns out this is not an issue with your code,revalidatePath, or the Next.js Cache configuration.

The Root Cause: This is a binary-level race condition in the React 19 Fiber Reconciler (specifically regarding resolveLazy and useId replay tracking). When a Server Action resolves very quickly, the reconciler marks the boundary as suspended but fails to "replay" the update to the DOM, leaving the UI stuck in a pending state even though the data has arrived on the client.

The issue was introduced in Next.js commit that upgraded React from eaee5308-20250728 to 9be531cd-20250729. Which was fixed in a [React Patch](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/35518) on Jan 17, 2026.

https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/86055
https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/35399

This is tracked in commit that created the issue in NextJs [e5c1dff8262b4d7dcef5bda0af9d9171196457bd](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/e5c1dff8262b4d7dcef5bda0af9d9171196457bd)

The Fixes:
I tested multiple approaches. You have two options depending on your risk tolerance:
Option 1: If you must use Next.js 16, you cannot stay on the stable release (as of this comment) because it bundles the affected React binary. You must force-install the specific React Canary build that contains the fix:
Bash

`npm install next@canary react@canary react-dom@canary --force
`
_Note: Ensure the installed react-dom version hash is from Jan 19, 2026 or later._

Option 2: What I did Since next@canary can be unstable for production, the safest path is to remove the buggy React 19 engine entirely. I downgraded to Next.js 15.3.6 and react 19.0.0
Result: The race condition does not exist in React 19.0.0 and React 18 The spinner works perfectly every time.

Security Note: If you downgrade, make sure to use next@15 (not an old specific patch) to ensure you are covered against [CVE-2025-66478](https://nextjs.org/blog/CVE-2025-66478).

TL;DR: It's a React 19 bug . Upgrade to the absolute latest Canary or downgrade to React 19.0.0 (Next.js 15 or Next.js 14) to solve it. Don't waste time debugging your revalidatePath logic.

body:
This is actually **expected behavior** in Next.js Parallel Routes. Here's why: ## How `default.tsx` Works in Parallel Routes When Next.js can't find a matching slot for a parallel route (like when you navigate to `/dashboard/kanban` but there's no `@navbar/kanban` directory), it falls back to `default.tsx`. However, `default.tsx` is treated as a **direct replacement for the slot content**, not as a page that goes through the slot's layout. ### The Behavior: 1. **With `/app/dashboard/@navbar/kanban/page.tsx` present:** - Renders: `@navbar/layout.tsx` → `@navbar/kanban/page.tsx` - Layout wrapper is applied ✅ 2. **Without the kanban directory (using `default.tsx`):** - Renders: `@navbar/default.tsx` directly - Layout wrapper is **NOT** applied ⚠️ ## Why This Happens `default.tsx` is designed to be a **fallback slot content**, not a page in the routing system. It's rendered directly into the slot without going through the segment's layout hierarchy. ## Solutions ### Option 1: Include Layout in `default.tsx` (Recommended) Wrap your default content with the layout explicitly: ```tsx // /app/dashboard/@navbar/default.tsx import NavbarLayout from './layout'; export default function Default() { return ( <>Default Navbar ) } ``` ### Option 2: Use Catch-all Route (Your Workaround) Your workaround using `[...default]/page.tsx` works because it's treated as an actual route segment, which does go through the layout: ```tsx // /app/dashboard/@navbar/[...default]/page.tsx export default function CatchAll() { return <>Default Navbar } ``` This makes it a proper page route, so the layout applies. ### Option 3: Move Layout Logic to Parent If the layout styling needs to be consistent, apply it at the parent layout level: ```tsx // /app/dashboard/layout.tsx export default function Layout(props: LayoutProps<'/dashboard'>) { return (
{props.navbar}
{props.children}
) } ``` ## Recommendation For your use case, **Option 2** (catch-all route) is cleanest since it maintains the routing hierarchy properly and allows the slot's layout to work as expected for all routes. ## Reference This behavior is documented in the [Next.js Parallel Routes documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/parallel-routes#defaultjs) under the `default.js` section.

body:
Likely a module that's being loaded? do you have any `window` references at top level scope in your project? Like:

```ts
// some js or ts file

import { } from 'somewhere'

const data = window.something

export function foo () {}
```

Maybe this file is getting loaded/required as part of a server run? Of course this doesn't explain why it doesn't happen with Node 20 at all, but good to check first.

body:
I think this is mostly a route-shape limitation, not a missing config flag.

Intercepting routes are matched by route segment depth. The `(.)` / `(..)` markers are relative to segments, and `@modal` does not count as a segment. A catch-all like `[[...slug]]` then makes the target ambiguous because it can consume any number of segments.

So this:

```txt
app/@modal/(.)[[...slug]]/page.tsx
```

does not mean "open a modal for any URL whose slug contains `annex`". It means "intercept the same-level catch-all route", but the router still has no concrete `annex/[id]` segment to match for the modal slot. That is why it starts working when you switch to a static route: the target segment and relative depth are known.

For this kind of CMS route I would pick one of these approaches:

1. Keep `app/[[...slug]]/page.tsx` as the canonical full-page CMS renderer, and render the modal from inside that page when `params.slug` contains `annex`. This is the simplest option if `annex` can appear at arbitrary depth.
2. Normalize annex pages to a predictable route shape, then intercept that concrete route. For example, if you can make annex URLs live at `/annex/[annexSlug]`, then use a normal page route plus `app/@modal/(.)annex/[annexSlug]/page.tsx`.
3. If you need multiple known depths, model those depths explicitly. I would avoid trying to make a single optional catch-all do this, because the intercepting matcher needs a concrete relative route shape.

Also keep `app/@modal/default.tsx` returning `null`; that handles the inactive slot state, but it will not make an arbitrary catch-all path interceptable by itself.

body:
This is a Next.js App Router routing error related to catch-all segments. Let me explain:

The Problem
You have a folder structure like this:
 app/
└── [locale]/
    └── (shop)/
        └── (category)/
            └── [...slugs]/
                └── opengraph-image.tsx  ❌ ERROR HERE 
The error says: "catch all segment must be the last segment"

Once you use [...slugs] (catch-all), you cannot have additional files/folders that create new path segments after it.

 Use API route for OG image instead
Create an API route and generate the image dynamically:

app/
└── api/
    └── og/
        └── route.tsx  ✅ Generate OG images here

Why This Happens
Catch-all segments ([...slugs]) capture everything in the URL path after that point. So Next.js can't know if /shop/category/product/opengraph-image means:

Route to opengraph-image.tsx file, OR
Route to catch-all with slugs = ["product", "opengraph-image"]

body:
This is a really common frustration with the App Router.

The issue is that in the App Router, any route with a dynamic segment (`[id]`) is automatically marked as **dynamic** unless Next.js can statically determine the route at build time. When you navigate to a dynamic route, Next.js needs to re-execute the server component tree to check if there's any dynamic data, which triggers that `_rsc` request you're seeing.

`use client` only tells Next.js where the component boundary is for client-side hydration — it doesn't change the route's rendering strategy. Even if the whole page is a client component, the router still treats it as dynamic.

Here are a couple things you can try:

1. **Use `generateStaticParams`** in your `[id]/page.tsx` to pre-generate the static routes at build time. This tells Next.js the exact set of `id` values, so it can render them as static pages without `_rsc` calls.

2. **Use `export const dynamic = 'force-static'`** in your page to force static generation (only works with `generateStaticParams`).

3. **Switch to a query param approach** instead of dynamic segments, like `/items?id=123`. This keeps the route static.

The Pages Router handled this more intuitively because it didn't mix server/client boundaries the same way. Hope this helps!
author: ezsouza

body:
The `?_rsc` calls on dynamic routes are **by design** in App Router — but there are concrete ways to eliminate or reduce them for your use case.

## Why dynamic routes always fire `?_rsc`

When you client-side navigate to a dynamic route (`/items/[id]`), Next.js fires a `?_rsc=...` fetch to re-run the **server component tree** for that route. This happens even if your `page.tsx` is `'use client'` — because:

1. Next.js still needs to resolve the **layout tree** server-side (layouts are always Server Components unless explicitly marked `'use client'`)
2. The App Router uses RSC for **all navigations** to dynamic segments to support server-side data, middleware, and layout nesting
3. `'use client'` only marks where client components start — the route itself is still "dynamic" because the segment is unknown at build time

## Solution 1: Add `generateStaticParams` (if IDs are known)

If your items have known IDs (or a known set), pre-generate them:

```typescript
// app/items/[id]/page.tsx
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const items = await fetchAllItems(); // or use a static list
  return items.map((item) => ({ id: item.id.toString() }));
}

export const dynamicParams = false; // 404 for unknown IDs (optional)
// or
export const dynamicParams = true;  // still SSR for unknown IDs
```

With `generateStaticParams`, known IDs become static — **no `_rsc` call** on navigation to pre-rendered pages.

## Solution 2: Force your layouts to be lightweight (the real fix for Tanstack Query)

Since you're using Tanstack Query client-side, the `_rsc` call is likely coming from a **Server Component layout** that does something (e.g., auth check, data fetch). Make all parent layouts minimal:

```typescript
// app/items/layout.tsx  — keep this a simple pass-through
export default function ItemsLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <>{children}</>;
}
```

Avoid any `async` operations in layouts above your dynamic route. The `_rsc` request cost is directly tied to how much work your server component tree does — if layouts are trivial pass-throughs, the 300-400ms drops dramatically.

## Solution 3: Use `loading.tsx` to mask the latency

If you can't eliminate the `_rsc` call, you can make it invisible:

```typescript
// app/items/[id]/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return <YourSkeletonComponent />; // shown immediately during _rsc fetch
}
```

This renders instantly while the `_rsc` request completes in the background — users see a skeleton, not a blank page or a 300-400ms freeze.

## Solution 4: `prefetch` on hover

If you're using `<Link>` to navigate to items, Next.js prefetches the `_rsc` payload **before** the user clicks:

```tsx
<Link href={`/items/${id}`} prefetch={true}>
  View Item
</Link>
```

With prefetching, the `_rsc` payload is already cached by the time the user navigates — **zero perceived latency**.

## Summary

| Approach | Eliminates `_rsc`? | Works with unknown IDs? |
|---|---|---|
| `generateStaticParams` | ✅ Yes | ❌ No (only known IDs) |
| Lightweight layouts | ❌ No, but much faster | ✅ Yes |
| `loading.tsx` skeleton | ❌ No, but invisible | ✅ Yes |
| `<Link prefetch>` | ❌ No, but pre-fetched | ✅ Yes |
| Query params (`?id=`) | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes (but changes URL structure) |

For a Tanstack Query app with unknown IDs at build time, the best combination is **lightweight layouts + `loading.tsx` + `<Link prefetch>`**. This makes the `_rsc` call fast and invisible without restructuring your routes.

body:
## Solution

This error means Linux has hit its maximum limit for file system watchers. Turbopack (and other tools like VS Code, webpack) need to watch many files for hot reload.

## Quick Fix (Temporary)

Increase the limit for your current session:
```bash
sudo sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288
sudo sysctl -p
```

Then restart your dev server.

## Permanent Fix (Recommended)

### Step 1: Edit sysctl.conf
```bash
sudo nano /etc/sysctl.conf
```

### Step 2: Add these lines at the end:
fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288
fs.inotify.max_user_instances=512

### Step 3: Apply the changes:
```bash
sudo sysctl -p
```

### Step 4: Verify:
```bash
cat /proc/sys/fs/inotify/max_user_watches
# Should output: 524288
```

## For Ubuntu/Debian Users

You can also create a dedicated config file:
```bash
echo "fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/40-max-user-watches.conf
sudo sysctl --system
```

## Why This Happens

- Default Linux limit: ~8,192 watches
- Large Next.js projects can have thousands of files
- Each file in `src/`, `app/`, `pages/`, and `node_modules` (when not excluded) needs a watcher
- Turbopack watches more aggressively for faster HMR

## Additional Optimization

Exclude unnecessary directories from watching in `next.config.js`:
```js
module.exports = {
  webpack: (config, { isServer }) => {
    config.watchOptions = {
      ignored: ['**/node_modules', '**/.git'],
    };
    return config;
  },
};
```

## Check Current Usage
```bash
# See how many watches are currently in use
find /proc/*/fd -lname anon_inode:inotify 2>/dev/null | cut -d/ -f3 | xargs -I {} sh -c 'cat /proc/{}/cmdline 2>/dev/null; echo' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
```

Hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions.

## Short Answer

**No, 15.5.10 does not exist as a patched version.** You should upgrade to **15.5.9** (the latest secure version in the 15.5.x line).

## Security Context

There have been **three critical security advisories** for Next.js in December 2025:

### 1. CVE-2025-66478 (CVSS 10.0 - Critical RCE)
- **Disclosure:** December 3, 2025
- **Impact:** Remote Code Execution via React Server Components
- **Affected:** Next.js 15.x, 16.x, and canary releases ≥14.3.0-canary.77
- **NOT affected:** Next.js 13.x, 14.x stable, Pages Router, Edge Runtime

### 2. CVE-2025-55184 / CVE-2025-67779 (High - DoS)
- **Disclosure:** December 11, 2025
- **Impact:** Denial of Service (infinite loop hangs server)
- **Affected:** All App Router applications ≥13.3

### 3. CVE-2025-55183 (Medium - Source Code Exposure)
- **Disclosure:** December 11, 2025
- **Impact:** Server Function source code can be leaked
- **Affected:** Next.js 15.x and 16.x only

## Recommended Safe Versions (As of January 2026)

| Your Version | Upgrade To |

body:
## Solution

This is a known issue with Turbopack on Windows when using Prisma. The error occurs because Turbopack tries to create symbolic links (junction points) that fail due to Windows permissions.

## Quick Fix

### Option 1: Run Terminal as Administrator

Close your terminal and reopen it with "Run as Administrator", then run:
```bash
npm run dev
```

### Option 2: Enable Developer Mode (Recommended)

This permanently allows symlink creation without admin rights:

1. Open **Settings** → **Update & Security** → **For Developers**
2. Enable **Developer Mode**
3. Restart your terminal
4. Run `npm run dev` again

### Option 3: Disable Turbopack Temporarily

If you need a quick workaround, run without Turbopack:
```bash
# Instead of: npm run dev (which uses --turbopack by default in Next.js 15+)
npx next dev --no-turbopack
```

Or modify your `package.json`:
```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "next dev --no-turbopack"
  }
}
```

### Option 4: Regenerate Prisma Client

Sometimes the Prisma client needs regeneration:
```bash
# Clear node_modules and regenerate
rm -rf node_modules/.prisma
rm -rf node_modules/@prisma
npx prisma generate
npm run dev
```

## Why This Happens

Turbopack uses symlinks for faster builds. On Windows:
- Symlinks require either Administrator privileges OR Developer Mode enabled
- Prisma's generated client has nested paths that trigger this

## Long-term Fix

The Next.js team is aware of this Windows-specific issue. Track progress:
- [GitHub Issue #62560](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/62560)

## Environment Check

Confirm your setup:
```bash
node -v      # Should be >= 18.17
npm -v       # Should be >= 9
npx prisma -v
```

Let me know if this resolves your issue!

- https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/cache-components#navigation-uses-activity

This keeps a number of routes (3) around, in the DOM, in React's new hidden mode (so-to-speak). More info in the Next.js docs. 

This issue is tracking feedback, workarounds, and more info, including likely upcoming changes: 

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/86577#issuecomment-3801284197 

Furthermore we have an upcoming Activity guide: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/89126

I'd say first understand what Activity is doing, from a pure React point of view, and then you can identify some way forward, or wait a bit until the gradual migration path lands. An official way forward is gaining traction, but as long as it is not published, it is best to work with what's available at the moment.

body:
Ran into this same thing a few weeks back. Turbopack doesn't support raw-loader the way webpack did. The rules config is pretty limited right now.

What worked for me:

**Option 1: fs at build time (server-side only)**

```tsx
import { readFileSync } from 'fs'
import { join } from 'path'

const svgContent = readFileSync(
  join(process.cwd(), 'assets/icon.svg'),
  'utf-8'
)
```

Works in server components and `getStaticProps` / `generateStaticParams`. Won't work client-side obviously.

**Option 2: fetch it client-side**

Move your SVGs to `/public` and load them at runtime:

```tsx
const [svg, setSvg] = useState('')

useEffect(() => {
  fetch('/icons/my-icon.svg')
    .then((r) => r.text())
    .then(setSvg)
}, [])
```

Then render with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` if you need the actual SVG in the DOM.

**Option 3: drop turbopack for now**

If you really need inline SVG strings at import time with `@svgr/webpack` or `raw-loader`, run `next dev` without `--turbo` until they add proper loader support. Turbopack is still catching up on some of these edge cases.

Not ideal but these are the workarounds that exist today.

Next.js package not found

This typically happens when Turbopack can't resolve the Next.js installation in your project.

```bash
# Remove node_modules and lock files
rm -rf node_modules
rm -rf .next

# Reinstall
npm install
```

### 2. Check Next.js Version

Your error shows `Next.js version: 0.0.0` - this indicates a broken installation.
```bash
# Verify Next.js is installed
npm ls next

# If missing or broken, reinstall
npm install next@latest
```

### 3. Turbopack Canary Mismatch

You're using `Turbopack v16.1.0-canary.19` - canary versions can have compatibility issues.
```bash
# Use stable version instead
npm install next@latest
```

Or if you need canary:
```bash
npm install next@canary
```

### 4. Check package.json

Ensure `next` is in your dependencies:
```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "next": "^14.x.x"  // or your target version
  }
}
```

### 5. Clear Turbopack Cache
```bash
rm -rf .next
rm -rf node_modules/.cache
npm run dev
```

---

## 🔧 If Still Not Working

Try disabling Turbopack temporarily:
```bash

body:
I think this is running into the HTTP status-code limitation of streaming rather than a normal `notFound()` bug.

With Cache Components enabled, reading `searchParams` is runtime data, so it has to happen under a Suspense boundary/static shell. Once that Suspense boundary starts streaming its fallback, the response has already committed as `200 OK`. If `notFound()` is called after that point, Next.js can still render the not-found UI and add the noindex behavior, but it cannot change the already-sent HTTP status to `404`.

So if the requirement is a real HTTP 404, the decision has to happen before streaming starts. In practice that means one of these patterns:

1. Validate the request earlier, before rendering the Suspense boundary, if the condition can be known without awaiting runtime data.
2. Move the route-shape validation out of the streamed page path, for example into `proxy`/middleware or a route handler that can return/redirect before the page render.
3. If the check depends on `searchParams`, avoid putting the `notFound()` decision behind a Suspense boundary when you need the actual HTTP status. Otherwise, accept that the streamed response will stay `200` and only the rendered UI/noindex state can change.

The relevant constraint is in the streaming guide: once streaming begins, headers/status are already sent, so `notFound()` mid-stream cannot retroactively turn the response into a 404.

https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/streaming#the-http-contract

body:
I think there's a few of layers to this discussion.

The fetch patching layer added by Next.js, won't be present if you do something like [this](https://undici.nodejs.org/#/?id=using-cache-interceptor).

The Next.js patch handles deduping, and it also adds data to the Data Cache, which you can use for time based revalidation, or on-demand tagged revalidation.

Now the bit that's interesting here too is that, Cache Components abstracts the caching layer, from internals, into the code you write, so you wouldn't necessarily need to use the fetch Data Cache, and you'd still have time based revalidation, or on-demand via tags.

I wonder if you are mixing up a few things here too... 

Performance differences, between either of the three options are likely to be negligible, say all things being equal you may expect axios to be slower, but it will be your implementation that dictates the overall performance, and memory management. Implementation being your client wrapper, and the way your data is fetched from source and passed to the client.

If you don't have a bottleneck or performance issue being solved, and are just considering migrating, the native/patched-by-next.js fetch should be alright.

Also, Node.js' fetch indeed does implement undici, but I don't necessarily see the connection to "therefore if I do mine in undici it will be faster". There's some interesting tooling in undici, left outside fetch for standard compliance and what not, but most apps don't need those, I'd say anyway.

body:
Ok, so this is intentional, even found a test for it, but my justification is as follows:

The top level (├ ◐ /[username]/posts): This is the route definition - the file that exists in your app directory.                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                         
Nested items (│ └ /[username]/posts): These show what was actually prerendered as static shells. In this case, a fallback static shell was generated for the dynamic pattern itself.     

This is more noticeable and helpful for permutations on routes with multiple dynamic segments. For example `/[category]/[slug]` in something like:                                                                         
  
```js                                                                                                                                                                      
  export function generateStaticParams() {                                                                                                                               
    return [                                                                                                                                                             
      { category: 'tech' },                    // partial - only category                                                                                                
      { category: 'tech', slug: 'intro' },     // complete                                                                                                               
      { category: 'sports', slug: 'news' },    // complete                                                                                                               
    ]                                                                                                                                                                    
  } 
```

Then I'd guess you see:

```console
  └ ◐ /[category]/[slug]                                                                                                                                                 
    ├ /[category]/[slug]    ← fallback shell (both params dynamic)                                                                                                       
    ├ /tech/[slug]          ← partial shell (category resolved, slug dynamic)                                                                                            
    ├ /tech/intro           ← fully prerendered                                                                                                                          
    └ /sports/news          ← fully prerendered   
```

`tech/[slug]` is not repeated, right, but a partial shell so-to-speak, in the same category as `[category]/[slug]`

body:
Hi @yusifaliyevpro! 

This is **not a bug**, but rather the expected build output format when using **Partial Prerendering (PPR)** .

The duplicate looking lines represent the two different phases of the route rendering:

1.  **The Parent Line** : Represents the **Static Shell** of the page. This is the initial HTML that gets served immediately from the cache/CDN.
2.  **The Indented Line** : Represents the **Dynamic Holes** (usually components wrapped in `<Suspense>`) that are streamed in dynamically after the shell loads.

The legend at the bottom confirms this with the **◐ symbol**:
> `(Partial Prerender) prerendered as static HTML with dynamic server-streamed content`

body:
This error usually means that Turbopack cannot correctly detect the project filesystem root and ends up treating `src/app/not-found.tsx` as if it were outside of the project.

First, make sure you are running the dev server from the actual Next.js project root. The directory where you run next dev should contain `package.json`, `next.config.js` (or `next.config.mjs`), and the `src/ folder` if you’re using the `src` directory. Running the command from a parent or nested folder often causes this exact error.

Also double-check that you are really using the App Router. The `not-found.tsx` file is only supported in the App Router (`app/` or `src/ap`p). If the project is using the Pages Router, this file will not be recognized correctly.

Another thing to look at is your `next.config`. Custom setups like monorepos, workspaces, or options such as `distDir` can confuse Turbopack if the project root does not match the location of `src/app`.

One thing that stands out is:

`Next.js version: 0.0.0`


This usually means the version could not be resolved properly or Next.js is being run from source. Reinstalling dependencies and making sure you are using an official Next.js release often fixes this.

As a quick workaround, you can try running the dev server with Webpack:

`next dev --webpack`


If that works, it confirms this is a Turbopack-specific issue rather than a problem with the file itself.

Overall, this doesn’t look like an issue with not-found.tsx, but rather a project root / filesystem detection problem in Turbopack.

body:
**Yes, this is currently expected behavior (Architecture Trade-off), but your observation on scaling is valid.**

### The "Why" (Intent)
In the App Router model, `app/not-found` and `app/error` are treated as part of the **Global Shell** availability. Since any route segment can potentially throw a 404 or an Error during streaming or navigation, Next.js eagerly preloads these fallback UI styles to ensure an **instant, layout-shift-free transition** to the error state.
* If these were lazy-loaded, a user hitting a 404 would likely see a blank screen or unstyled content while the browser fetches the new chunk, degrading the UX during a critical failure moment.

### The Optimization Gap
However, you are absolutely right that for large applications, blocking the *critical path* of the successful render to optimize for the *failure path* is a suboptimal trade-off (Lighthouse impact).

### Recommendations
1.  **Immediate Mitigation:** Ensure your `not-found.tsx` is extremely lightweight. Avoid importing heavy UI libraries in that specific file; stick to Tailwind utility classes or inline styles to keep that hoisted chunk minimal.
2.  **Next Steps:** Since you mentioned interest in prototyping a heuristic tweak , **you should definitely open a Feature Request Issue** with your findings. The core team would likely be open to moving these "universal routes" to a non-blocking loading strategy.

Hope this clarifies the "Intent" vs "Side effect" question
author: Dagris

body:
Thanks for the clarification that makes sense.
I understand the intent behind treating app/not-found / app/error as part of the global shell to guarantee an instant, layout-shift-free transition during streaming or navigation failures.

My concern is mostly about the scaling trade-off, not the behavior itself. As apps grow, prioritizing the failure path on the critical render path of every successful route starts to become noticeable especially with:

- Render-blocking unused CSS
- Growing shared CSS chunks
- Lighthouse blocking time regressions
- fallback CSS being prioritized ahead of route-critical styles


I agree that lazy-loading error UI entirely would be a UX regression, but there may be a middle ground worth exploring for example:

- lower-priority preload (or non-blocking stylesheet) for universal error routes

- deferring error-route CSS until after route-critical CSS is applied

- or a heuristic/opt-out for applications that accept a brief fallback flash in exchange for better steady-state performance


I’ll open a dedicated feature request to explore this more formally and attach reproduction details + measurements.
Happy to prototype or experiment with a heuristic tweak if there’s interest from the core team.

Thanks again for confirming the intent this helped a lot in understanding whether this was a bug or an architectural trade-off.

body:
## ✅ SOLUTION: Duplicate Icon Files in App Directory

I encountered the exact same error and found the root cause. This Turbopack panic occurs when you have **multiple icon files with the same base name** in your `app/` directory.

### The Problem

Next.js metadata file-based API doesn't support having both `icon.png` and `icon.svg` (or `icon.jpg`, etc.) in the same directory. When Turbopack processes these duplicate icons during build, it triggers the "Dependency tracking is disabled" panic.

### How to Fix

**Option 1: Keep only one icon format** (Recommended)
```bash
# Keep SVG (scalable, smaller file size)
rm app/icon.png

# OR keep PNG
rm app/icon.svg
```

**Option 2: Move extra icons to `public/` directory**
```bash
mv app/icon.png public/icon.png
# Then reference it in your code as /icon.png
```

**Option 3: Use different names if you need multiple icons**
```bash
mv app/icon.png app/app-icon.png
# or
mv app/apple-icon.png public/apple-icon.png
```

### Verify the Issue

Check for duplicate icons in your app directory:
```bash
ls -la app/icon.* app/apple-icon.* app/favicon.*
```

### After the fix:
```bash
rm -rf .next
pnpm build
```

### Why This Happens

Next.js uses [file-based metadata conventions](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/metadata/app-icons) where `app/icon.(png|jpg|svg)` automatically generates `<link>` tags. Having multiple files with the same base name creates conflicts in Turbopack's dependency tracking system.

### Workaround if you must keep using Turbopack

If the above doesn't work, disable Turbopack for builds:
```json
// package.json
"scripts": {
  "build": "next build --webpack"
}
```

---

**Update:** Confirmed this fixes the issue in Next.js 16.1.4 and 16.1.6. The error completely disappears after removing duplicate icon files.

body:
A few migration lessons from moving larger apps to Next.js 16:

* I'd avoid putting `"use cache"` on pages. Pages work best as orchestration layers.
* Put `"use cache"` on data-fetching functions or cached child Server Components.
* Create a central cache tag registry early. It becomes much easier to reason about invalidation once the app grows.
* If you're coming from `unstable_cache`, let Next.js handle cache keys. The biggest mindset shift is that arguments and closures are auto-keyed now.

For PPR, yes, it works well with Cache Components, but be careful around request-time APIs (`cookies()`, `headers()`, auth, params/searchParams usage). Most of the weird bugs I've debugged after migrating ended up being cache-boundary issues rather than caching itself.

For data that updates every few minutes, I'd generally use:

```ts id="v9z2m1"
"use cache";
cacheLife("minutes");
cacheTag(...)
```

rather than thinking in ISR terms. The cache model is much more explicit now.

I ended up documenting the architecture, migration path from `unstable_cache`, cache tags, revalidation patterns, personalized content, search params, and debugging steps here:

https://www.skills.sh/mohamed-hossam1/nextjs-cache-architecture/nextjs-cache-architecture

Code examples:
https://github.com/mohamed-hossam1/nextjs-skills

Might save you some migration pain. If it does, a ⭐ on the repo would be appreciated.

body:
Before opening this discussion, I tried the Vercel Docs AI bot, but it hallucinated quite a bit. After digging further myself, I found the following explanation:

When a page is dynamically rendered, it executes as a `Vercel Function`. In this scenario, the Function’s response headers take precedence over any headers defined in `next.config.ts`. Because Vercel Functions have higher priority, headers configured at the framework level are effectively ignored for dynamic routes.

This also aligns with your point about vendor lock-in:
> Self-hosting behaves as expected because there’s no vendor lock-in and you retain full control. However, when deploying to a vendor platform, platform-specific behavior applies.

In other words, this isn’t a Next.js limitation—it’s a Vercel platform–specific behavior, where the runtime overrides framework-level header configuration for dynamic routes.

So if we want reliable control over cache behavior, we should rely on `Next.js–provided mechanisms` (SSG, ISR, fetch caching, route segment config, etc.) instead of manually setting Cache-Control headers, since those headers ignored once the route is executed as a Vercel Function.

body:
This feels out of scope for Next.js / create-next-app. 

Next.js is styling-agnostic, and Tailwind is explicitly mobile-first by design (min-width breakpoints). 

This is essentially asking Next.js to maintain a workaround for using Tailwind in a way Tailwind itself doesn’t promote. That should live as a community template, not in the default scaffolding.

- https://tailwindcss.com/docs/responsive-design#working-mobile-first
- https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/discussions/15653

Adding and maintaining extra “desktop-first” CSS scaffolding in create-next-app would be ongoing maintenance burden and would bake a particular styling philosophy into the framework template.

And yes, the vast majority of projects is likely using Tailwind, but I don't have any data on how many prefer a desktop-first variant out of the box. 

If there’s a need for a desktop-first workflow, it likely belongs upstream as a Tailwind discussion, a community template / starter, or even a showcase in this very discussions section. 

`create-next-app` should stay minimal and avoid shipping extra CSS conventions it would need to support long-term.
author: icyJoseph

body:
Thanks for the detailed explanation—I really appreciate you taking the time to outline those concerns.

I totally agree that create-next-app should remain lean and styling-agnostic. My intention wasn't to alter the default philosophy, but rather to propose an entirely optional, opt-in flag (default: false).

Here was my reasoning:

**Zero Impact on Defaults:** Those who wanted the traditional mobile-first Tailwind workflow wouldn't be impacted at all.

**Convenience for Specific Projects:** This would be a "quality of life" flag for teams working on desktop-first designs (e.g., complex dashboards) who wanted to quickly scaffold that workflow. It would simply offer a tiny utility layer without actually changing how Tailwind works.

That being said, I totally understand your point about the maintenance overhead. If even an optional flag is too much for the core scaffolding to handle, I totally get it.

That error is suggesting you have something like:

```text
src/app
├── [[...lang]]
│   └── (cart)
│       └── cart
│           └── route.ts

```console
Invalid segment Static("cart"), catch all segment must be the last segment modifying the path
(segments: [OptionalCatchAll("lang"), Group("cart")])
```

There can be multiple ways to trigger this, but the root cause is the same.

`[[...lang]]` **must be the last element in the path**, and nothing (static or dynamic) can come after it.

The issue described in CVE‑2026‑23864 is a denial‑of‑service vulnerability in React Server Component (App Router) server functions. It affects Next.js versions 13–14.x because the App Router proxies requests through an internal server component boundary; a specially crafted request can tie up the server.

The key points I found when reviewing the advisory and Vercel’s response:

  *   Only the App Router is impacted. The Pages Router and traditional SSR pages are not affected because they don’t expose the same server function API. If you can temporarily switch to the Pages Router for affected routes, that mitigates the issue.
  *   No fix is being backported to v14. According to the maintainers, v14 is end‑of‑life. The patched versions begin at v15.0.8 and later (15.1.12, 15.2.9, 15.3.9, 15.4.11, 15.5.10, 15.6.0‑canary.61, 16.0.11 and 16.1.5). There will be no security release for v14.
  *   Recommended mitigation: upgrade to one of the patched versions of Next.js 15 or 16. If you cannot upgrade immediately, the only practical workaround is to disable the App Router or wrap the application behind a Web Application Firewall / rate limiter to block malicious requests. Since the vulnerability allows an attacker to consume CPU time but not to execute arbitrary code, a WAF can detect and drop the long‑running requests.

So the path forward is either (a) migrate to the Pages Router on v14, or (b) schedule an upgrade to v15+ where this CVE has been fixed. There is unfortunately no way to safely continue using the App Router on v14 without these mitigations.
