body:
The roundtrip isn't what you're optimizing away. What differs between client and server fetch is **what re-renders** and **who owns the cache**, not whether a network call happens. So the choice is about ownership and invalidation, not latency-elimination.

A deep tree of cheap server components costs nothing to re-render. The cost is **where you `await`**. If you `await searchParams` or a fetch high up, the whole page render *blocks* on it. If you pass the un-awaited promise down and `await` it inside one small Suspense wrapped subtree, the shell flushes immediately, with fallback UI, the subtree data streams alter. 

**Isolate the await behind a Suspense boundary as low as possible.** See, https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/streaming#push-dynamic-access-down.

There's a couple choices to make here:

**`<Suspense key={id} fallback={<Skeleton/>}>`**

Changing the key remounts the boundary. It's a fresh mount with no "already-revealed content". The **the fallback shows on every `id` change.** You get a skeleton flash each time. Good when each `id` is a genuinely different thing and a clear "loading the new thing" signal is what you want.

**Wrap the navigation in a transition**

React's rule: *it will not hide already-revealed content with a fallback during a transition.* So if the table is already on screen and the transition causes the server component to suspend, React **keeps the old table visible** and just flips `isPending` true. You dim the table / show a spinner via `isPending`, old data stays put until new data streams in. 

Pick one:
- If you need to "show me a skeleton each time", then key it.
- If you want to "keep the table, while it is refreshing", then use `isPending`.

`<Link>` and router navigations are **already** transitions internally, so for soft-nav param changes you get this pending behavior for free. If you want an explicit pending flag you can either `useTransition` around a manual `router.push`, or use Next 16's `useLinkStatus` for `<Link>`-driven loading state. 


| Goal                                  | Tool                                                     |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Don't block the shell on the fetch    | pass un-awaited promise down, `await` low                |
| Stream the slow part in               | `<Suspense>` around that subtree                         |
| Skeleton on every id change           | `<Suspense key={id}>`                                    |
| Keep old table, show "refreshing"     | no key + `isPending` (`useTransition` / `useLinkStatus`) |
| Don't even re-render the static shell | Cache Components (cached shell + dynamic PPR hole)       |

All of these are still "server fetch + roundtrip", they're just about *hiding* the roundtrip well. Client fetch (SWR/React Query) remains the escape hatch when the data is browser-state/real-time/interaction-gated, at the cost of owning the cache.

---

And a side note, a Client Component can be parent (not rendering owner) of a Server component: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#interleaving-server-and-client-components

As said before, there'll likely be an API to do what you are thinking about, in the short/medium term future, but for now, the above applies.

body:
This is a PostCSS subprocess crash. Turbopack spawns a Node.js child process to transform CSS via PostCSS, and that process is dying with "unexpected end of file" -- it starts writing a response packet then terminates mid-frame.
Most likely causes (check in order):
1. PostCSS config error -- postcss.config.js/.mjs throws at runtime. Test directly: node -e "require('./postcss.config.js')" from project root. Common culprits: missing plugin, invalid syntax in the config, or a plugin that calls a browser-only API.
2. Tailwind v4 with @import "tailwindcss" -- if you're using Tailwind v4's new @import syntax in globals.css, the classic tailwindcss PostCSS plugin is incompatible with it. Either downgrade to @tailwind base/components/utilities directives, or remove the PostCSS plugin and use Tailwind v4's Vite/lightningcss integration instead.
3. Node.js version mismatch -- Turbopack's PostCSS subprocess uses your system Node.js. If you have a version that's too old or has a broken stdio pipe (common with nvm/nodenv shims), the IPC packet reading fails. Run node --version and ensure it matches the version in your .nvmrc/engines field.
4. Corrupt node_modules -- rm -rf node_modules .next && npm install to rule out a bad .cache or partial install.
The @tailwindcss/postcss plugin (require('@tailwindcss/postcss')) is the #1 cause right now because Turbopack expects the legacy tailwindcss plugin interface; the v4 plugin has a different init path that crashes the child process.

body:
You are reading the docs correctly. As of 16.2.9 the caching guide still shows the `<Suspense>` boundary above `<body>` as the way to opt the whole document out of the static shell, so the pattern itself is intended, not a docs typo.

Two things worth separating though. Moving `<body>` outside the boundary is not a harmless fix: with `<html><body><Suspense>{children}</Suspense></body></html>` you are back to prerendering a static shell (the document tags themselves), and only the children are deferred. Depending on why you opted out that may be perfectly fine, but it is not the same behavior as the documented snippet, which defers everything to request time.

The error you are seeing looks like the root layout validation not accounting for a boundary sitting between `html` and `body`, which the render itself handles fine. That matches icyJoseph's comment about a bug in this exact pattern that got fixed. So before restructuring the layout I would check which version you are on and try the latest 16.2 patch (or a recent canary) with the documented snippet unchanged. If the error still fires on latest, then the validator and the docs genuinely disagree and it is worth filing as a bug with a minimal repro, because one of the two needs to change.

body:
This is a module resolution error -- Turbopack can't find the next package on disk when building its server import map.
Most likely cause: you're using pnpm and the project root isn't where pnpm's virtual store resolves. Turbopack resolves next relative to the project root, and if node_modules/next (or the pnpm store link) doesn't exist at that exact path, you get "Next.js package not found."
Try these in order:
1. rm -rf node_modules .next && npm install (or pnpm install --shamefully-hoist if using pnpm)
2. If that doesn't work, check that node_modules/next actually exists and isn't a dangling symlink: ls -la node_modules/next
3. Make sure you're running next dev from the same directory that has node_modules as a direct child -- not a workspace subdirectory without its own install
4. If you're in a monorepo (turborepo, nx, etc.), add next to the root package.json dependencies so it's hoisted, or run the command from the app directory that has its own node_modules/.pnpm store
The "Next.js package not found" string comes from get_next_server_import_map in Turbopack's next-api crate -- it literally does a require.resolve('next') at project init. If that throws, nothing else works.
author: Senthil455

body:
This error means Turbopack can't find the Next.js package on disk. Common causes:
1. Missing dependency install -- Run npm install / pnpm install / yarn in the project root.
2. Monorepo without hoisting -- If using a monorepo (pnpm workspaces, turborepo, nx), check that next is listed as a dependency and the packages are installed. With pnpm, you may need to configure node-linker=hoisted in .npmrc or use pnpm install --shamefully-hoist.
3. Path resolution issue -- Turbopack resolves the Next.js package at startup. If node_modules/next is a symlink (pnpm default) and the target doesn't exist, you'll get this. Try node -e "require('next')" to verify Node can find it.
4. Corrupted node_modules -- Delete node_modules and lockfile, then reinstall.
Start with node -e "console.log(require.resolve('next'))" to see where it's resolving from, then verify that path actually exists.

This is a **Turbopack cache corruption** issue. The incremental build database inside `.next` got corrupted (usually from a crashed or force-killed process).

## Fix 1 — clear the cache (try this first)

```bash
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
```

## Fix 2 — clear node_modules cache too

```bash
rm -rf .next node_modules/.cache
npm run dev
```

## Fix 3 — disable Turbopack temporarily

In `package.json`, remove the `--turbo` flag:

```json
"scripts": {
  "dev": "next dev"
}
```

## Why this happens

Turbopack stores incremental task data in a local database. If the process is killed mid-write, the database can end up in a corrupted state. Deleting `.next` forces a full clean rebuild.

> Note: Your Next.js version shows `0.0.0` which suggests a canary or local build — worth reporting at [github.com/vercel/next.js/issues](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues) with Turbopack version `23c46498`.

body:
**Yes — Next.js is completely independent of Vercel.** Vercel maintains it, but it's open source and runs anywhere. You have two main self-hosting paths, and which one works on a "shared server" depends on whether that host lets you run a Node.js process.

### Option 1 — Node.js server (supports *all* Next.js features)
If your host can run a long-running Node process, just build and start it:

```bash
npm run build
npm run start   # runs `next start`
```

This supports everything: SSR, API routes, ISR, image optimization, middleware, etc. Works on any VPS or Node-capable host (DigitalOcean, AWS EC2, Hetzner, Railway, Render, a self-managed Linux box, etc.). For smaller/Docker deployments, set `output: 'standalone'` in `next.config.js` — it produces a minimal `.next/standalone` folder with a `server.js` you can run with `node server.js`, no `node_modules` install needed.

### Option 2 — Static export (works on basic/cheap shared hosting)
If you're on traditional shared hosting (cPanel, Apache/Nginx, PHP-style hosts) that **only serves static files and can't run Node**, use a static export:

```js
// next.config.js
const nextConfig = {
  output: 'export',
}
module.exports = nextConfig
```

`next build` then generates an `out/` folder of plain HTML/CSS/JS you can upload to any static host (shared hosting, S3, Nginx, Apache, GitHub Pages, etc.).

> ⚠️ The trade-off: static export drops features that need a server at runtime — SSR, API routes/Route Handlers, on-demand ISR, middleware, and built-in Image Optimization. If you need those, you need a Node host (Option 1).

### Quick decision guide
- **Cheap/shared host, static files only** → `output: 'export'` (Option 2).
- **Host that runs Node / VPS / Docker** → `next build && next start` or `output: 'standalone'` (Option 1, full features).

So the short answer: yes, you can host it anywhere — a basic shared server works with a static export, and any Node-capable server runs the full app.

Hope this resolves it — if so, would you mind clicking **"Mark as answer"** so others searching for the same thing can find it quickly? Happy to clarify further.

Small correction on Option 2 — a lot of shared hosts running cPanel actually *can* run Node, not just static files. cPanel ships with a **"Setup Node.js App"** feature: you set the application root, the startup file (e.g. `server.js`), the Node version, and run `npm install` right from the UI. So you can run a Next.js custom server there, not only a static export.

A couple of caveats worth flagging:
- It depends on the host having Passenger/Node enabled — not every cheap cPanel plan exposes it, so check the interface first.
- With a custom `server.js` you do lose some of Next.js's built-in optimizations (Image Optimization, some ISR behavior), so it's a trade-off vs. just running `next start` on a proper Node host/VPS.

And +1 on being careful about what you expose — make sure `package.json`, `.git/`, `.env` and `node_modules` aren't reachable from the public URL. Passenger keeps the app root separate from the document root, which helps, but it's worth double-checking your `public_html` / web root anyway.

body:
Yes, you can absolutely host and deploy a Next.js application on a shared server, VPS, or any other hosting provider independent of Vercel. Next.js is not locked into Vercel and offers multiple deployment strategies.

Here are the primary options depending on your hosting setup:

### 1. Static HTML Export (SSG) - Works on ANY Shared Hosting (e.g., Hostinger, Bluehost, cPanel)
If your app does not rely on Node.js server-side features (like dynamic server-side rendering `getServerSideProps` or App Router dynamic API routes), you can export it as static HTML:
1. Update your `next.config.js` / `next.config.mjs`:
   ```javascript
   const nextConfig = {
     output: 'export',
   };
   ```
2. Run `npm run build` (or `pnpm build` / `yarn build`).
3. This creates an `out` folder containing pure HTML, CSS, and JS files.
4. Upload the contents of the `out` folder to your shared hosting's public directory (e.g., `public_html`) via FTP or cPanel File Manager.

### 2. Shared Hosting with Node.js Support
Some modern shared hosting providers support Node.js applications (often managed via cPanel's **Setup Node.js App** feature):
1. Build the application locally or on the server: `npm run build`.
2. Upload the project files (including `.next`, `public`, `package.json`, and `node_modules`).
3. Configure the Node.js application in cPanel, pointing the startup file to the Next.js custom server script (or using `node_modules/next/dist/bin/next` as the application entry point).

### 3. Self-Hosting on a VPS (AWS, DigitalOcean, Linode, etc.)
This is the recommended approach for dynamic Next.js applications because it gives you full control and supports all features (including SSR, ISR, and API routes):
* **With Node.js:** 
  1. Install Node.js on your server.
  2. Clone your repository, run `npm install`, and `npm run build`.
  3. Start the application in production: `npm run start` (or manage the process using `pm2` to keep it running in the background: `pm2 start npm --name "next-app" -- start`).
  4. Use a reverse proxy like **Nginx** or **Apache** to route traffic from port 80/443 to port 3000.
* **With Docker (Recommended for production):**
  Next.js provides an official Dockerfile template. You can build a Docker image of your app and deploy it on any server supporting Docker or container runners.

### 4. Alternative PaaS Hosting (Serverless / Managed Node)
If you want a managed hosting experience similar to Vercel without using Vercel, you can use:
* **Render**, **Railway**, or **Fly.io** (Simply link your GitHub repository, and they will automatically build and deploy it using Node.js or Docker).
* **Netlify** (Offers native support for Next.js and serverless functions).
* **AWS Amplify** or **SST** (Deploys Next.js to AWS using Lambda and CloudFront).

- You need SSH access and the ability to run `npm run build` and keep `node server.js` running

### 3. Static Export (if no server features needed)
- Use `output: "export"` in next.config.js to generate pure HTML/CSS/JS
- Works on **any** static hosting (Apache, Nginx, shared hosting, GitHub Pages)
- Limitation: No API routes, no SSR, no server-side features

### 4. Self-hosted with Docker
```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = { output: "standalone" }
```
```bash
next build
cd .next/standalone
node server.js
```

## Recommendation
For a production app needing SSR/API routes, use a **VPS** (not shared hosting). If you only need static pages, use `output: "export"` and any hosting will work.

body:
There are two different behaviors involved here, and that is where most of the confusion comes from:

1. **Request memoization during a render pass**
   - In the current docs, only **`GET`** `fetch` requests are automatically memoized in the React component tree.
   - So a `POST` request is **not memoized** the way repeated `GET` requests are.
   - Route Handlers are also outside the React component tree, so that memoization rule does not apply there either.

2. **Persistent caching / Data Cache behavior**
   - In the current `fetch` docs, the default is effectively **not force-cached** (`auto no cache`).
   - If you want a request to be cached, you need to opt in with things like `cache: 'force-cache'`, `next.revalidate`, or route-level cache config such as `fetchCache`.

So for the concrete case people usually mean:

```ts
await fetch(url, { method: 'POST' })
```

You should treat that as:
- **not memoized**, and
- **not cached by default**

unless you explicitly opt into caching behavior.

The two relevant doc sections are:
- `fetch` API reference: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch
- caching guide: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components

I agree this would be worth stating explicitly in the `fetch` docs because users often read “fetch caching” and “fetch memoization” as the same thing when they are not.
author: JeremyZeng77

body:
**Yes - a `POST` request *can* be stored in the Data Cache, but only when you explicitly opt in with `cache: 'force-cache'`.** It is not cached by default.

By default (Next.js 15+), `fetch` isn't cached at all, and `POST` is excluded a second time because only `GET`/`HEAD` are treated as cacheable methods (the internal `isUnCacheableMethod` check). So a plain `POST` always hits the network.

When you pass `cache: 'force-cache'`, Next.js sets `finalRevalidate = INFINITE_CACHE`, which makes `isCacheableRevalidate` true, and the cache-write branch then runs **for the `POST` response too**. So your example *will* be written to the Data Cache, and `next.tags: ['property']` works as expected — you can purge it later with `revalidateTag('property')`.

Conditions that must hold for the `POST` to actually be cached:

- The response status is **`200`** (non-200 responses are not stored).
- The fetch is **not** inside a Route Handler that uses `POST`, and **not** inside a Server Action — those are never cached.
- No request-time/dynamic APIs (`cookies()`, `headers()`) ran above it in a way that forces the route dynamic.
- The cache key incorporates a hash of the request **body**, so different payloads are cached as separate entries (important for the GraphQL-over-POST use case).

```ts
// Cached in the Data Cache, revalidatable by tag
fetch('https://some-api.com', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({ somePayload }),
  cache: 'force-cache',
  next: { tags: ['property'] },
})
```

One caveat worth noting: with `GET` + `force-cache`, requests carrying `Authorization`/`Cookie` headers can still pass the caching checks, which is arguably a separate bug - but for the `POST` + `force-cache` question, the behavior is intentional and the response is cached.

> **Note:** this describes the fetch-level caching model. If you're on Next.js 16 with **Cache Components** / the `use cache` directive, caching is opt-in via `use cache` instead and these `fetch` cache semantics change.

Hope this fully resolves the question - if it does, would you mind clicking **"Mark as answer"** so others searching for the same thing can find it quickly? Happy to clarify anything further.
author: logusivam

body:
**Short answer: yes.** A `POST` request *is* stored in the Data Cache, but only when you explicitly opt in. 

The key thing to keep in mind: caching is opt-in for every request. A `fetch` is written to the Data Cache when **all** of these hold:

- It runs server side
- **Draft Mode** is not enabled (draft mode bypasses the cache and calls the real endpoint).
- **Explicit opt in** to caching with `cache: 'force-cache'`, or `next: { revalidate: N }` where `N > 0` (or `false` for indefinite), or a route-level `export const fetchCache` / `dynamic`.
- Response status is **`200`**.

> Tags only attach invalidation metadata to a request that is *already* cacheable (via `force-cache` or `revalidate`). A `POST` with only `next: { tags: ['property'] }` and no `cache`/`revalidate` is **not** cached. In your snippet it's cached because of `cache: 'force-cache'`; the tag just lets you later call `revalidateTag('property', 'max')`.

The cache key includes the URL, method, headers, `mode`, `redirect`, `credentials`, `referrer`, `referrerPolicy`, `integrity`, `cache`, and the **request body**, so two `POST`s with different payloads are stored as separate entries.

> [!NOTE]
> With Cache Components, `caching directives` make it easier to model this as: "caching the outputs of functions", rather than some option on a patched primitive. That being said, you can still use both. One benefit of that is that the fetch cache key doesn't use the deploymentId, so you can actually protect upstream resources, across deployments. This is ongoing development, IIRC, eventually cache directives should support this too.

I'll see to add some minimal diff to the fetch docs to cover this.

> There have been multiple discussions and questions about this topic, but there still doesn't seem to be a clear, definitive answer that users can easily find.

This is partly because, the initial behavior, cache by default, while the framework specifically opted-out in some cases, which forced you to opt those back into the caching... Teh simpler model as said about, is to opt-in, as you see fit, regardless of method or whatever else. There's some very tiny caveats here and there, but I ain't gonna touch that right now.

It also looks like there's a bit of v13/14 code paths that don't work anymore, but when answering LLMs see them, and attempt to build these contrived claims. Even reference `revalidateTag` with a single argument, and so on...

````md I think your understanding is correct: the EdgeWorker is modifying the HTML after Next.js has already produced the server-rendered React tree, but React still hydrates using the tree it expects from the original render. So from React’s point of view, the server/client tree is still something like: ```tsx
', }} /> ```` But the browser DOM at hydration time has become: ```html
Dynamic Banner Content
``` That means React is hydrating a DOM structure it did not render. During hydration/reconciliation, React can remove or replace the injected content because that content is inside a React-owned subtree. I would not expect `suppressHydrationWarning` to solve this. It can silence some hydration warnings, but it does not mean “do not hydrate this subtree” or “preserve whatever external HTML was inserted here”. It is not really an ownership boundary. As far as I know, there is no supported App Router API that marks a region inside the React tree as permanently outside React ownership. If the node is rendered by your React/Next app, React should be treated as owning that node and its children. The safer patterns are: ### 1. Let Next render the final banner HTML If possible, move the personalization decision before the Next render. For example, the EdgeWorker/CDN can set a header or cookie, and the Next.js Server Component can render the correct banner during SSR. Example idea: ```tsx import { headers } from "next/headers" export default async function Page() { const h = await headers() const bannerVariant = h.get("x-banner-variant") const bannerHtml = await getBannerHtml(bannerVariant) return (
) } ``` In this approach, the HTML React hydrates is the same HTML React expects. That avoids the mismatch because the banner is part of the actual React server output. ### 2. Keep the initial React output stable, then inject after hydration If the banner must be loaded separately, another option is to render a stable empty slot and fill it on the client after hydration. ```tsx "use client" import { useEffect, useRef } from "react" export function BannerSlot() { const ref = useRef(null) useEffect(() => { async function loadBanner() { const res = await fetch("/banner-url") const html = await res.text() if (ref.current) { ref.current.innerHTML = html } } loadBanner() }, []) return
} ``` This avoids the hydration mismatch because React initially renders the same empty `
` on both the server and client. The injected HTML is added only after hydration. The tradeoff is that the banner is no longer fully edge-injected before hydration, and you need to be careful with sanitization/CSP if inserting raw HTML. ### 3. Put the edge-injected content outside the React root If the content must be inserted at the edge before the browser receives the HTML, then the most reliable way is to inject it outside the DOM region that React hydrates. For example, the CDN/EdgeWorker could insert a banner before or after the app root, or into a separate container that React never renders into. Inside the App Router tree, though, this is hard to guarantee because React/Next owns the rendered app structure. ### What I would avoid I would avoid this pattern: ```tsx
', }} /> ``` and then replacing that markup at the edge with real banner HTML. That creates a mismatch by design. The browser sees the edge-modified HTML, but React hydrates using the original React output. So the short answer is: * `suppressHydrationWarning` will not make React ignore the subtree. * There is no supported “outside React ownership” marker for a subtree inside the App Router tree. * If the banner must survive hydration, either render it through Next/React during SSR, inject it after hydration, or place it outside the hydrated React root. * For edge-side personalization, a good pattern is often: EdgeWorker decides the variant → passes it via header/cookie → Next renders the matching banner HTML. Hope this helps. ``` ```

body:
Not sure why this was closed and reopened, but from the behavior described, this looks expected in the App Router rather than a bug.

For dynamic routes, `revalidate` alone does not always mean unknown slugs will be generated on first request and cached like ISR. Next needs the route to be statically generatable.

For large blogs/products/catalogs, this pattern works well:

```tsx
export const revalidate = 86400
export const dynamicParams = true

export async function generateStaticParams() {
  return []
}
```

This means no slugs are generated at build time, unknown slugs are allowed at runtime, and the page can be generated on first request, cached, and revalidated later.

Just make sure the route is not forced dynamic by things like `cache: "no-store"`, `dynamic = "force-dynamic"`, or request-specific usage like `cookies()` / `headers()`.

So yes, for dynamic App Router ISR, using `generateStaticParams()` with an empty array is a valid pattern when you want on-demand generation plus caching for unknown slugs.

If this solves your case, marking it as the answer can help others find it faster.

body:
A couple of the suggestions above (`NEXT_DISABLE_MEMORY_LIMIT`, `experimental.turbopackMemoryLimit`) don't seem to be real Next.js config options as far as I can find in the current docs/source — worth double-checking before adding them, they likely won't do anything.

The two real knobs for this in 16.x are:
- `experimental.turbopackMemoryEviction` (`false | 'full'`, defaults to `'full'`) — controls how aggressively Turbopack drops cached data between snapshots when the persistent filesystem cache is on (`turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev`, also on by default). If it's explicitly set to `false` somewhere in your config, that's your leak.
- `experimental.webpackMemoryOptimizations` — only applies if you're actually on Webpack, not Turbopack, so skip it if you're on the v16 default.

Since you're on Windows 11, the two most common causes I've run into aren't Next-specific at all:
1. Windows Defender real-time scanning the project folder — `.next` and `node_modules` get rewritten constantly by the dev server, and Defender re-scanning every write is a big RAM/CPU sink. Add an exclusion for the repo folder.
2. If the project lives inside OneDrive (or Dropbox), the sync client fights the file watcher for every change under `.next/dev`, which compounds badly with Turbopack's persistent cache. Moving the project outside any synced folder usually fixes it outright.

If it's still climbing after ruling those out, there's an actual measurement path instead of guessing: run with `NODE_OPTIONS=--inspect next dev`, connect Chrome DevTools, and take a couple of heap snapshots a few minutes apart to see what's actually retained. `NEXT_TURBOPACK_TRACING=1` also generates a trace you can load at trace.nextjs.org, which shows whether it's genuinely Turbopack's cache growing or something in your own code (e.g. an uncleared interval/websocket in a layout).

body:
A follow up with what actually checks out in current Next.js source, since a couple of the earlier suggestions don't hold up.

`NEXT_DISABLE_MEMORY_LIMIT` isn't a real Next.js environment variable, there's no reference to it anywhere in the vercel/next.js source.

`experimental.turbopackMemoryLimit` is real though. It's defined in `packages/next/src/server/config-shared.ts` as `turbopackMemoryLimit?: number`, documented as "a target memory limit for turbo, in bytes", nested under `experimental`.

Since Next.js 16.2.6 runs `next dev` on Turbopack by default (`packages/next/src/lib/bundler.ts`: "the default is turbopack when nothing is configured"), most of the classic webpack memory advice in the official guide (nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/memory-usage) doesn't really apply here, disabling the webpack cache or `experimental.webpackMemoryOptimizations` are webpack specific.

Two Turbopack specific things worth checking:

Project location relative to lockfiles. Turbopack infers its watch root from the nearest `pnpm-lock.yaml` / `package-lock.json` / `yarn.lock` / `bun.lock(b)`. If the project sits inside a monorepo or a nested folder with a lockfile in a parent directory, Turbopack ends up watching and resolving from that broader tree, increasing memory pressure. Tracked in #94432 ("Turbopack inferred parent root causes high memory pressure in next dev"), still open. Setting `turbopack: { root: path.join(__dirname) }` explicitly to the actual app directory avoids the broader scan.

There's also an open report of unbounded memory growth from HMR retaining old module instances across repeated recompiles on both Turbopack and webpack in 16.2.x (#94696), auto closed by the repro-link bot rather than triaged, worth a thumbs up or a fresh issue if the pattern matches (RAM climbing steadily with every save, flattening after a dev server restart).

A concrete next step: run `NODE_OPTIONS=--inspect next dev`, connect Chrome DevTools' memory tab to the exposed port, and take two heap snapshots a good number of saves apart. That narrows it down quickly between monorepo root scanning, HMR retention, or something project specific.
author: MILLERMARRU

body:
This is a known issue with Next.js dev server. Here are some solutions:

**1. Limit Node.js memory**

Add `--max-old-space-size=4096` to your dev script:

```json
"scripts": {
  "dev": "node --max-old-space-size=4096 node_modules/.bin/next dev"
}
```

**2. Disable turbopack if using it**

Turbopack can cause memory leaks in some cases:

```bash
next dev  # instead of next dev --turbopack
```

**3. Clear .next folder regularly**

```bash
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
```

**4. Exclude large folders from file watching**

In `next.config.js`:

```js
module.exports = {
  webpack: (config) => {
    config.watchOptions = {
      ignored: [**/node_modules, **/.next, **/public]
    }
    return config
  }
}
```

**5. Update Node.js**

You are using Node.js 24 which is very new. Try LTS version 20 or 22:

```bash
nvm install 20
nvm use 20
npm run dev
```

**6. Use WSL2 instead of Windows**

If you are on Windows, file watching is much faster in WSL2:

```bash
wsl
cd /mnt/c/your-project
npm run dev
```

**7. Check for memory leaks in your code**

- Avoid importing large modules at the top level
- Use dynamic imports for heavy components
- Check for infinite re-renders or state updates

If the issue persists, try creating a minimal reproduction and opening an issue on GitHub.

body:
high ram in the next.js dev server usually comes from one of these three things.

first, the incremental compiler keeps module graphs in memory and they grow as you visit more pages. set `experimental.workerThreads: false` in next.config to disable workers if you are on a tight machine, or cap the node heap:

```
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=1024" npm run dev
```

second, check your imports. barrel files like `import { x } from "../components"` where that index re-exports 40 things force the compiler to load the whole barrel even if you only need one export. switch to direct imports and you will see a noticeable drop.

third, if you are on next.js 14+, turbopack is the default dev compiler. it is generally faster but its memory profile differs from webpack. try switching to the webpack compiler to compare:

```
npx next dev --turbo=false
```

also look for any custom webpack plugins in `next.config.js` that might be holding references. running `node --inspect` and opening chrome devtools heap snapshots is the most reliable way to find what is actually keeping memory alive.

body:
I think this is the most thoughtful answer here. 

I also think it is worth clarifying a few things, that I think get lost in the rush to get an answer marked. 

As OP's snippet is presented, the server generates HTML and RSC, as it is, without any need to re-evaluate strings client side, so the claim that there's a hydration error there is not founded. 

However, this still means that the locale used to format that string, is bound to whatever the Node.js process, on the server, is configured with. There are ways to change this, and arguably, you should have your server's TZ and locale etc, configured when developing too. 

The problem happens when the HTML contains Client Component output, because the JavaScript to replay the compoennt is now also Client side, it runs again for hydration. All of the functions that have impure behavior, or side-effects, or whose results depend on the environment, are going to be problematic. In rare cases, suppressing the error and moving on, could be acceptable, a small timestamp and such, but generally it is best to fix these, hydration issues can break event listeners and what not. 

Notably here, this isn't an issue of `App Router`, but `Client Components`~everything pre RSC~, that is, even Pages Router, or any SSR framework that attempts to render a Server driven first frame, to start interactivity from, in the client, deals with this. React's just strict on this, because it attaches event listeners, and if the next node in the JavaScript representation of the tree, is a button, but React encounters a div, we have a problem. _And once again, the Next.js dev overlay, highlights, the node, difference and recommends docs for possible fixes._

There are several ways to handle this, it almost always depends on what your intent is. For example, [toLocaleString](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/toLocaleString#using_locales), may receive a `locale` argument, and `options`, one of which is the [timeZone](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/toLocaleString#using_options) - so you can already, regardless of browser/server drift, render the correct thing server side, given that you make the decision upfront for the user (same for all users, sub group of users, config driven, etc).

With Cache Components, you can also opt-into, the Suspense-ful behavior, because Date operations are unstable, you need to use cache, or ship a fallback instead, which wraps a Client Component that uses Date. There's guidance on how to do this in the upcoming 16.3 release, as soon as you use Date, and the framework requires you to make a decision, you'll be guided along.

I am also working on a Hydration Issues guide. Even though, the hydration issue story is, for the vast majority of cases, well resolved and documented. We point at the stack, with + and - indicating the Server, Client mismatch, and the error page you get sent to has improved over time. My reasoning for a guide is that you kind of want to also, not run into this, and your agent shouldn't spend tokens on fixing these, it should be knowledge you reason about with from the start, easily.

We have also published a guide about flashing UI: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/preventing-flash-before-hydration#dates-and-formatting

One problem with the `setMounted` approach, over what's presented here, via a transitions, is that it can incur in heavy re-rendering, and cause other issues with other transitions. Without `startTransition`, it is a high priority update.

body:
Your instinct is right that you can't set the header from `page.tsx`, but the reason matters: by the time a Server Component renders, Next may already be streaming the response, so the headers are gone. It's not an arbitrary limitation, it's a consequence of streaming.

How you solve it depends on what the `Cache-Tag` is actually for.

**If you want Next's own cache to be tag-invalidatable**, skip the header entirely. Tag the fetch and let Next track it:

```ts
const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/page/${slug}`, {
  next: { tags: [`article_${articleId}`] },
})
```

Then invalidate with `revalidateTag('article_10')` from a Server Action or route handler whenever that article changes. No header wrangling, and it works with the Full Route Cache.

**If you specifically need the `Cache-Tag` response header for an external CDN** (Fastly surrogate keys, Cloudflare cache tags, etc.), that's where middleware comes back in, and you can kill the double-fetch you were worried about. Have middleware do the API call, then rewrite to the page while passing the result down as a request header:

```ts
// middleware.ts
const data = await fetch(apiUrl).then(r => r.json())
const res = NextResponse.rewrite(req.nextUrl, {
  request: { headers: new Headers({ 'x-article-id': String(data.article_id) }) },
})
res.headers.set('Cache-Tag', `article_${data.article_id}`)
return res
```

Now `page.tsx` reads the id off `headers()` instead of fetching again, and the CDN gets its tag. One API call, header set where it's actually allowed.

One thing that won't work: `headers()` in `next.config.js`. That's static only, so it can't do per-article values.

If it's the second case, the middleware-passes-data-down pattern is the standard way people handle surrogate keys on Next today.

body:
Your approach looks broadly aligned with how App Router and RSC are intended to work. Using react.cache() as the mechanism for creating a request-scoped container is a sensible choice because it provides request-local memoization and allows nested Server Components to share the same container during a render.
The strongest part of the design is keeping the DI container on the server and passing only serializable state snapshots to the client. That fits naturally with RSC boundaries and avoids the complexity of mirroring server-side services in the browser.
The main thing to be careful about is disposal. Route Handlers and Server Actions have clear lifecycle boundaries, so explicit cleanup there makes sense. However, React currently doesn't expose a reliable "render finished" hook for Server Components, so deterministic disposal after an RSC render is difficult to guarantee.
For progressive state delivery, I'd lean on React/Next.js streaming and Suspense rather than building a custom snapshot-streaming mechanism. Overall, the architecture feels well thought out, framework-friendly, and consistent with current RSC semantics.
author: Ishant1302

body:
This is basically the right shape. `cache()` is exactly the primitive you want for a per-request container: it memoizes for the life of one server request and throws the cache away between requests, so "one child container per request" falls out for free without you tracking request IDs yourself. Nice fit.

Two things I'd flag before you lean on it too hard:

**`cache()` only reaches the render tree.** It dedupes within a single RSC render pass. Server Actions and Route Handlers don't run inside that tree, so a `cache()`-backed container won't be the same instance you get during render. If someone expects `getContainer()` in a Server Action to hand back the same child container the page used, it won't, and that's a fun one to debug at 2am. Worth calling out loudly in the docs.

**`AsyncLocalStorage` is the complement, not the competitor.** It's the other request-scoped primitive in Node, and it covers the spots `cache()` can't reach (middleware, route handlers, plain server code). It's less React-idiomatic and a bit more ceremony, but if you ever need one container that's truly consistent across render *and* actions *and* handlers in the same request, that's the tool. Might be worth a "when to reach for which" note.

The "only pass serializable snapshots to the client" rule is the right call and honestly the part people get wrong most, so good that it's baked in from the start.

I opened a follow-up PR based on your comments:

What changed:

- kept `React.cache()` as the primitive for RSC render scope;
- documented that Page/RSC containers are not shared with Server Actions or Route Handlers;
- updated Route Handler and Server Action examples to use an explicit request scope;
- added a separate `di-craft/node` adapter backed by `AsyncLocalStorage` for Node async contexts outside the RSC render tree;
- kept the client boundary as `server state -> serializable snapshot -> client state`.

```txt
RSC render scope   -> di-craft/next/server -> React.cache()
Node async scope   -> di-craft/node        -> AsyncLocalStorage
Client boundary    -> serializable snapshots
```

body:
I think this depends a lot on what we mean by “i18n support”.

Pages Router did have something closer to a built-in i18n API, mainly around routing. But from the feedback the team collected back then, it seemed like many apps still had to customize or work around it once they needed specific locale detection behavior, fallback logic, URL structures, translation loading, CMS integration, pluralization, interpolation, type safety, etc. 

So while the Pages Router API looked more “complete” on the surface, a non-trivial number of projects still ended up customizing the i18n layer anyway.

App Router gives you primitives to build the setup that fits your app. And this is also an area where the primitives can keep improving. For example, with upcoming [root params support](https://preview.nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params), accessing something like a locale segment from shared server code won't need prop drilling it through every layout/page boundary.

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/internationalization

I do think a setup option, example, or starter template could help reduce friction. But I’d be careful about framing this as first-party multilingual support unless the scope is clear. Things like routing conventions, locale-aware examples, proxy patterns, and primitives like root-params feel like a good fit for Next.js, while message formatting, pluralization, interpolation, extraction, translation management, and type-safety choices feel more like things specialised libraries are better suited for.

body:
Hi @samselikoff! Testing 16.3 Preview with Turbopack + `output: "standalone"` — found a real bug with `turbopackIgnore`.

```
Warning: Dynamic filesystem access causes tracing of the whole project
```

This **cannot be silenced** when a filesystem call receives a `path.join(...)` expression as its argument — even though the warning message itself recommends exactly that placement as the fix.

This has been originally reported here: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/95125

<details>
<summary>Additional details</summary>

## 📁 Minimal Reproduction

```js
// lib/loader.js
import fs from 'fs'
import path from 'path'

const folder = path.join(process.cwd(), 'data')

// ✅ WORKS — bare variable, comment silences warning
const files = fs.readdirSync(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ folder)

// ❌ STILL WARNS — no comment placement can silence this
const contents = files.map(f =>
  fs.readFileSync(path.join(folder, f), 'utf8')
)

// ❌ STILL WARNS — this is the EXACT form the warning recommends!
const contents2 = files.map(f =>
  fs.readFileSync(path.join(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ folder, f), 'utf8')
)

// ❌ STILL WARNS
const contents3 = files.map(f =>
  fs.readFileSync(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ path.join(folder, f), 'utf8')
)
```

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. Create the file above in a Next.js 16.3 canary project
2. Add `output: 'standalone'` to `next.config.js`
3. Run `next build` (default Turbopack)
4. Observe — `readFileSync(path.join(...))` cannot be silenced

---

## 📊 Annotation Behavior Matrix

| Annotation Placement | Result |
|---|---|
| `readdirSync(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ folder)` | ✅ Silenced |
| `readFileSync(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ path.join(folder, f))` | ❌ Still warns |
| `readFileSync(path.join(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ folder, f))` | ❌ Still warns |
| `readFileSync(path.join(folder, f))` — no comment | ❌ Warns |

> **The warning message says to use** `path.join(/*turbopackIgnore: true*/ process.cwd(), bar)` —
> **but this form does not work** for the outer `readFileSync` call.

---

## 🔍 Root Cause (Traced in Source)

After digging into the Turbopack source, the exact bug is in:

**`turbopack/crates/turbopack-ecmascript/src/references/mod.rs` — line ~1554**

```rust
// All call arguments are always linked with EMPTY ImportAttributes
// The `ignore` flag is NEVER passed down to argument expressions
let linked_args = || async {
    linked_args_cache.get_or_try_init(|| async {
        unlinked_args
            .iter()
            .map(|arg| arg.clone_in(state.arena.get_or_default()))
            .map(|arg| state.link_value(arg, ImportAttributes::empty_ref()))  // ← BUG
            .try_join()
            .await
    }).await
};
```

**What this means:**

- `/* turbopackIgnore: true */` placed before a `path.join(...)` argument → the `ignore` flag is stored for the **`path.join` call's own span**
- When `readFileSync` evaluates its arguments, it uses `ImportAttributes::empty_ref()` (no ignore)
- The `path.join(...)` argument is evaluated as **dynamic** → `FsReadMethod` handler traces the whole project → warning emitted

The `ignore` flag only works on a **bare variable** (`readdirSync(/* turbopackIgnore: true */ folder)`) because that converts the **function itself** to `Unknown`, skipping the handler entirely.

---

## 💥 Why It Matters (Not Just Cosmetic)

This is a real deployment risk in these common cases:

**1. Runtime-resolved data folders:**
```js
// You CANNOT silence this no matter what
const data = fs.readFileSync(path.join(process.cwd(), 'data', filename), 'utf8')
```

**2. Libraries in `node_modules` (e.g. `drizzle-orm`'s `migrate()`):**
```js
// Inside node_modules — you cannot add comments here at all
const files = fs.readdirSync(migrationsFolder)
files.map(f => fs.readFileSync(path.join(migrationsFolder, f)))
```

**Result:** The entire project — including the `public/` folder — is traced into the standalone output. This can:
- Bloat deployment size significantly
- **Cause deployment failures** when serverless size limits are exceeded (Vercel, AWS Lambda, etc.)

---

## 🌍 Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| **Next.js** | 16.3.0-canary.65 (latest) |
| **Builder** | Turbopack (default) |
| **Config** | `output: 'standalone'` |
| **Node** | 22.x |
| **Platform** | macOS arm64 / Windows x64 |

---

## 🔗 Related Issues

- **#95125** — Full bug report with reproduction repo and detailed code analysis
- **#92639** — Earlier report of same family (auto-closed for invalid repro link, never triaged)

---

## ✅ Expected Behavior

The `/* turbopackIgnore: true */` placement shown in the warning message should actually suppress the trace — **or** the warning message should be updated to point to a placement that actually works.

---

## 💡 Proposed Fix Direction

In `references/mod.rs`, the `FsReadMethod` and `FsReadDir` handlers inside `handle_well_known_function_call` should:

1. Check `attributes.ignore` and return early (like `handle_dynamic_import` does at line ~1633)
2. **OR** propagate `ignore` status through argument linking so nested `path.join` calls are also suppressed

Happy to submit a PR if that would help! 🙏

</details>

body:
Hi, thanks for giving this a go!

If I understand your description correctly, this is expected, and it is the kind of case Instant Insights helps developers with.

An `/app/loading.tsx` boundary does apply to the route tree below the root layout, that's correct. On a initial page load, you'd see the loading UI, given that there's uncached or runtime data in the destination page.

This is not the same for client navigations. On a client navigation, re-render doesn't necessarily happen from the root. It re-enters the tree at the shared layout boundary between the current route and the destination route. The root Suspense boundary be above that shared layout, and it is not used in that navigation.

That Instant Insight is letting you know that navigating into this route "blocks", because the route is likely accessing uncached data or runtime data access, and there's no the boundary in any of the shared layouts, to guarantee a instant UI. The dev overlay points exactly at what the issue is.

author: Olulanke-Mainasara

body:
The `loading.tsx` file is a convention for wrapping a route segment in a Suspense boundary. Before Cache Components, it also allowed Next.js to prefetch up to that boundary. But it was a blunt tool, and one that could be hard to place correctly.

With Cache Components, you can place a Suspense fallback anywhere in the component tree. The framework detects blocking work and only shows the fallback when that work is actually encountered. More importantly, it can tell you when navigated-to work would block, letting you decide whether to wrap it in a fallback, cache it, or explicitly allow and acknowledge the block.

So looking only at the difference between `loading.tsx` and Suspense is perhaps not the right way to frame it. The `loading.tsx` convention exists to wrap a segment in a Suspense boundary without forcing you to refactor your page into an intermediary component, such as `BlogPage` and `BlogPageImpl`, where the only reason for the split is to put Suspense around the place where `params` are accessed.

One of the biggest improvements is around “work that can be navigated into, but would block.” You can now wrap exactly that work, and no more, in a Suspense boundary. That lets you reveal more of the page sooner, instead of hiding an entire route segment behind a broader fallback.

This does not mean `loading.tsx` goes away. It just makes it a clear segment-level Suspense wrapping convention, rather than the main tool for deciding how much of a navigation should be revealed.

author: Mad-Kat

body:
The Rust React Compiler is very new, and I think the whole JS/React ecosystem is figuring out how to integrate it.
The reason we were able to integrate it so easily into Turbopack is because we own the whole application, and we don't mind directly linking the code into our binary. It would be different to integrate the react compiler directly into SWC -- see, for example, oxc adding and then removing it recently.

SWC recently took ownership of the compiler crates that use it as the parser / transformer. They'll figure out the right way (direct integration vs plugins) to integrate it into projects that use SWC as a binary. I've personally compiled the React Compiler to a WASM plugin and it worked well, but it has a long cold startup time.
When they have a recommendation, we'll try to make it available to webpack Next.js users.

Hey! A few questions regarding the [blog post for 16.3](https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-3-instant-navigations):

1.) `use cache`
> The user will instantly see a previously cached UI (reused between requests).

1.1) The data of `use cache` is not persisted in any way, so where does it live? In memory? But for how long? There has to be some limit, right?
1.2) What happens for the first request to something that is marked with `use cache`? In other words, how is it filled initially? Or is the initial request blocking?

2.) Partial prerendering, cached shell and layout
> Instead of prefetching a page per link, Next.js will now prefetch a reusable shell per route.

The example used in the blog is for a route `/chat/[id]`. And as far as I understand: We "cache" everything statically until the first "async" operation or a `Suspense` boundary is encountered.

2.1) This is how partial prerendering worked for months already (before 16.3), right? Has something changed for that behavior?
2.2) I understand that the prefetched shell now happens for the whole route (`/chat/[id]`), instead of for all paths that exist as `<Link>`s on the page. author: bennettdams

body:
> The data of `use cache` is not persisted in any way, so where does it live? In memory? But for how long? There has to be some limit, right?

If the cached UI has a server-side lifetime, it will get prerendered and persisted to ISR. If it has a client-side lifetime, it will get "persisted" to the client-side cache. In either (or both) cases the lifetime is what lets Next show it instantly. (Server-side lifetime is controlled by the `cacheLife.expire` property and client-side lifetime is controlled by `cacheLife.stale`.)

> What happens for the first request to something that is marked with use cache? In other words, how is it filled initially? Or is the initial request blocking?

If it's the initial page load and the cached UI was statically prerendered, it will load it from the ISR cache (a CDN if you're on a platform that's using Adapters or the filesystem if you're self hosting). In either case we consider that "instant" because it's a static prerendered page, even though you will of course have to wait for the network to fetch the file. (In the future if we offline cache these then it would truly be instant even for page loads.)

For the first client-side navigation to a page, how the client-side cache gets filled depends on which Link you use. By default a `<Link>` only prefetches the route shell (and you can grow that shell by "use cache"ing content that does't depend on params). If you want to prefetch more of a page, you can use `<Link prefetch>` to include its params (and you can grow that prefetch by "use cache"ing more of that content). Once you actually navigate, all cached content ends up in the client-side cache and will therefore be available instantly for subsequent visits to the page.

> as far as I understand: We "cache" everything statically until the first "async" operation or a Suspense boundary is encountered

Yes, here you're describing the "static shell". (It's a little confusing because these static shells are different from the reusable shells mentioned in the post.) The static shell is indeed everything up to the first Suspense boundary (as well as any content you've given a server-side lifetime to with "use cache"). The behavior up to now has been that all Links on the page prefetch this static shell by default—the reasoning being, it's static content, therefore it's fast and cheap to prefetch, so let's do it for every link. What we found is that even though that's true, it could lead to your app prefetching _the same_ static shell for 20 chat links on a page, when in reality that static UI could be reused across all 20 links. No need to issue 20 separate requests. That's what the partial prefetching feature is all about.

> Isn't layout exactly the tool for static shells that can be "cached" and re-used for all paths of a route?

Layout is for UI that lives above a page (e.g. a sidebar of chats in a chatbot app). It is "re-used" in the sense that it doesn't rerender as you navigate between different chats. But here we're talking about the actual page-level UI itself. Maybe a loading spinner (for a chatbot-style app), maybe a skeleton screen for a dashboard. That UI belongs to the page and it's what we're bringing more sensible prefetching behavior to.

Basically, if a skeleton screen for a transaction in a banking app is the same for every transaction, we now only prefetch that once, and reuse it across all transactions.

---

Let me know if that makes sense or if you have any follow-ups! I want to share some demos walking through all this very soon, I'm hoping that will help drive some of these APIs home.

body:
I asked Fable 5, this is his response:

### **The issue**

After migrating to Next.js 16, components rendered via the Storyblok (CMS) appear twice on the page. The first copy is dead, stale server HTML - not connected to React (invisible in React DevTools), not interactive. The second copy below it is the real, working component.

Next 16 made Turbopack the default bundler. Under Turbopack, the Pages Router never emits dynamicIds in __NEXT_DATA__, which is the mechanism that preloads next/dynamic({ ssr: true }) modules before hydration. All our components are registered through next/dynamic, so React hydrates before the component module is loaded, the client tree doesn't match the server HTML, and React abandons the server-rendered DOM - leaving the orphaned duplicate. Verified: server HTML contains the component exactly once; __NEXT_DATA__.dynamicIds is absent under Turbopack but present under --webpack, where the bug doesn't reproduce.

Why we can't fix it properly

This is an upstream Turbopack bug, not something in our code - any next/dynamic({ ssr: true }) component is affected. Reproduced on next@16.2.9 and the latest next@16.3.0-preview.5, so no available upgrade resolves it. Until Vercel emits dynamicIds (or equivalent preloading) for the Pages Router under Turbopack, the options are only workarounds: static imports (bundle-size cost), React.lazy + Suspense (bypasses Next's manifests), or building with --webpack.

body:
# Review: Next.js App Router CSS Chunking — Community Answer Fact-Check

**Verdict:** Directionally reasonable, but it understates what's actually configurable. The claim "no supported configuration exists" is the weakest part — `experimental.cssChunking` is a real, documented option that directly addresses this.

---

## 1. CSS chunking control

**Claim:** No supported config to force CSS into separate files or prevent merging.

**Verdict:** ❌ Partially wrong.

`experimental.cssChunking` in `next.config.js` controls exactly this:

```js
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    cssChunking: 'strict', // try this first
  },
}
```

- **`true` (default):** Next.js merges CSS aggressively based on import-graph analysis to minimize requests. This is almost certainly *why* the homepage is pulling in other components' CSS.
- **`'strict'`:** Loads CSS in exact import order instead of merging — more/smaller chunks, but no cross-route leakage. **This is the one most likely to fix the reported issue.**
- **`false`:** Disables chunking entirely — one large bundle (worse for this use case).

This is the single biggest gap in the original answer. Test `'strict'` before concluding nothing is configurable.

---

## 2. Webpack / custom plugins

**Claim:** Not supported, may break across releases.

**Verdict:** ✅ Correct.

The App Router's CSS pipeline runs through internal loaders/plugins tied to the build, and Turbopack increasingly handles CSS through its own internals that don't route through the standard webpack config at all. A hand-rolled competing extraction plugin is not realistically maintainable long-term. Good practical advice as written.

---

## 3. Relation to issue #64773

**Claim:** Yes, closely related.

**Verdict:** ✅ Correct, but worth being precise.

The actual fix (PR `vercel/next.js#67373`, by sokra) addressed **global CSS leaking across chunk groups** — specifically styles applied to unscoped selectors (e.g. `body`) rather than CSS Modules classes. The fix disallows merging global CSS with styles from other chunk groups, because the old chunking logic assumed all CSS only affects the elements it's meant to (an assumption CSS Modules enforce but plain global stylesheets don't).

That's relevant background, but it's **narrower** than "unrelated component CSS leaking into route bundles" — which is a broader, still-open complaint:

- One developer found that with a catch-all route, enabling `cssChunking` caused routes *outside* the catch-all to pull in CSS they didn't need.
- Another reported the chunking feature causing chunks to contain CSS unrelated to the current page — enough to trigger Lighthouse's "unused CSS" warning — with disabling the feature resolving it.

That second report matches the symptom described almost exactly, and it's still being discussed as unresolved in general form.

---

## 4. Recommendations (lean layouts, CSS Modules, route groups, dynamic imports)

**Claim:** Reasonable hygiene practices.

**Verdict:** ⚠️ Reasonable but incomplete — omits the two most directly relevant levers:

- **`experimental.cssChunking: 'strict'`** (see #1)
- **`experimental.inlineCss`** — replaces `<link>` stylesheet tags with inline `<style>` tags in the `<head>`. Aimed squarely at "load only critical CSS," but:
  - Works best with atomic CSS (Tailwind) — output stays small regardless of how much UI grows.
  - Skip it if returning visitors matter — inlined CSS can't be cached separately from HTML and re-downloads every visit.
  - For larger CSS bundles, it increases TTFB since all CSS ships with every HTML response.
  - It does run on App Router (unlike `optimizeCss`/Critters — see below): supports both Webpack and Turbopack, with CSS precedence/deduping handled automatically by React 19.

```js
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    inlineCss: true, // all-or-nothing; not just "critical" CSS
  },
}
```

---

## 5. "No officially supported way to load only critical CSS while deferring dynamic component CSS"

**Verdict:** ✅ Correct — this is the honest bottom line.

True per-component critical-CSS extraction (à la Critters) is **not supported on App Router**: the `optimizeCss`/Critters approach relies on a library that doesn't support streaming, which is fundamental to how App Router renders. A Vercel team member confirmed this directly in the GitHub discussion. `inlineCss` is the closest sanctioned tool, but it's all-or-nothing (inlines *everything*, not just critical rules) and still experimental / not recommended for production per current docs.

---

## Recommended next steps, in order

1. **Set `experimental.cssChunking: 'strict'`** and rebuild. Check whether the homepage bundle shrinks. Free to try, most likely fix for the described leakage.
2. **Audit for global, unscoped selectors** (styles on `body`, bare tags, or anything outside a CSS Modules class) — these are exactly what merges indiscriminately under the old chunking assumption.
3. **If using Tailwind/atomic CSS,** consider `experimental.inlineCss` for pages with mostly first-time visitors. Skip it if you depend on stylesheet caching for returning users.
4. **For anything deeper** (manual critical-CSS extraction, fine-grained chunk control), treat it as a userland post-build step (e.g. Beasties/Critters run against static output) rather than a Next.js config knob — and expect it to be fragile across Next.js versions, same conclusion as the original answer.

> 
> - **`'strict'`:** Loads CSS in exact import order instead of merging — more/smaller chunks, but no cross-route leakage. **This is the one most likely to fix the reported issue.**
> 
> - **`false`:** Disables chunking entirely — one large bundle (worse for this use case).
> 
> 
> 
> This is the single biggest gap in the original answer. Test `'strict'` before concluding nothing is configurable.
> 
> 
> 
> ---
> 
> 
> 
> ## 2. Webpack / custom plugins
> 
> 
> 
> **Claim:** Not supported, may break across releases.
> 
> 
> 
> **Verdict:** ✅ Correct.
> 
> 
> 
> The App Router's CSS pipeline runs through internal loaders/plugins tied to the build, and Turbopack increasingly handles CSS through its own internals that don't route through the standard webpack config at all. A hand-rolled competing extraction plugin is not realistically maintainable long-term. Good practical advice as written.
> 
> 
> 
> ---
> 
> 
> 
> ## 3. Relation to issue #64773
> 
> 
> 
> **Claim:** Yes, closely related.
> 
> 
> 
> **Verdict:** ✅ Correct, but worth being precise.
> 
> 
> 
> The actual fix (PR `vercel/next.js#67373`, by sokra) addressed **global CSS leaking across chunk groups** — specifically styles applied to unscoped selectors (e.g. `body`) rather than CSS Modules classes. The fix disallows merging global CSS with styles from other chunk groups, because the old chunking logic assumed all CSS only affects the elements it's meant to (an assumption CSS Modules enforce but plain global stylesheets don't).
> 
> 
> 
> That's relevant background, but it's **narrower** than "unrelated component CSS leaking into route bundles" — which is a broader, still-open complaint:
> 
> 
> 
> - One developer found that with a catch-all route, enabling `cssChunking` caused routes *outside* the catch-all to pull in CSS they didn't need.
> 
> - Another reported the chunking feature causing chunks to contain CSS unrelated to the current page — enough to trigger Lighthouse's "unused CSS" warning — with disabling the feature resolving it.
> 
> 
> 
> That second report matches the symptom described almost exactly, and it's still being discussed as unresolved in general form.
> 
> 
> 
> ---
> 
> 
> 
> ## 4. Recommendations (lean layouts, CSS Modules, route groups, dynamic imports)
> 
> 
> 
> **Claim:** Reasonable hygiene practices.
> 
> 
> 
> **Verdict:** ⚠️ Reasonable but incomplete — omits the two most directly relevant levers:
> 
> 
> 
> - **`experimental.cssChunking: 'strict'`** (see #1)
> 
> - **`experimental.inlineCss`** — replaces `<link>` stylesheet tags with inline `<style>` tags in the `<head>`. Aimed squarely at "load only critical CSS," but:
> 
>   - Works best with atomic CSS (Tailwind) — output stays small regardless of how much UI grows.
> 
>   - Skip it if returning visitors matter — inlined CSS can't be cached separately from HTML and re-downloads every visit.
> 
>   - For larger CSS bundles, it increases TTFB since all CSS ships with every HTML response.
> 
>   - It does run on App Router (unlike `optimizeCss`/Critters — see below): supports both Webpack and Turbopack, with CSS precedence/deduping handled automatically by React 19.
> 
> 
> 
> ```js
> 
> const nextConfig = {
> 
>   experimental: {
> 
>     inlineCss: true, // all-or-nothing; not just "critical" CSS
> 
>   },
> 
> }
> 
> ```
> 
> 
> 
> ---
> 
> 
> 
> ## 5. "No officially supported way to load only critical CSS while deferring dynamic component CSS"
> 
> 
> 
> **Verdict:** ✅ Correct — this is the honest bottom line.
> 
> 
> 
> True per-component critical-CSS extraction (à la Critters) is **not supported on App Router**: the `optimizeCss`/Critters approach relies on a library that doesn't support streaming, which is fundamental to how App Router renders. A Vercel team member confirmed this directly in the GitHub discussion. `inlineCss` is the closest sanctioned tool, but it's all-or-nothing (inlines *everything*, not just critical rules) and still experimental / not recommended for production per current docs.
> 
> 
> 
> ---
> 
> 
> 
> ## Recommended next steps, in order
> 
> 
> 
> 1. **Set `experimental.cssChunking: 'strict'`** and rebuild. Check whether the homepage bundle shrinks. Free to try, most likely fix for the described leakage.
> 
> 2. **Audit for global, unscoped selectors** (styles on `body`, bare tags, or anything outside a CSS Modules class) — these are exactly what merges indiscriminately under the old chunking assumption.
> 
> 3. **If using Tailwind/atomic CSS,** consider `experimental.inlineCss` for pages with mostly first-time visitors. Skip it if you depend on stylesheet caching for returning users.
> 
> 4. **For anything deeper** (manual critical-CSS extraction, fine-grained chunk control), treat it as a userland post-build step (e.g. Beasties/Critters run against static output) rather than a Next.js config knob — and expect it to be fragile across Next.js versions, same conclusion as the original answer.

It is not true that setting cssChuncing: true will reduce css bundle size.
author: ChellappanRajan

body:
CSS Chunking can intentionally lead to overshipping "unreleated" css to other pages. This is done to reduce the number of requests needed for pages (since they have a cost too).

We recently added a new css chunking mode `experimental.cssChunking: { type: "graph" }` which adds more options to control the heuristic how much overshipping it accepts.

**Update: opened a fix PR — #95242.**

Root cause located in the Turbopack emitter (`crates/next-api/src/server_actions.rs`): `filename` and `exportedName` are stored both at the action-entry level (correct) **and** redundantly inside every per-page `ActionManifestWorkerEntry`. Since those strings are invariant per action and the worker map has one entry per reachable page, they get repeated `O(actions × pages)` times — the dominant cost of the 170MB+ manifest.

The PR drops the two redundant per-worker fields so worker entries are just `{ moduleId, async }`, matching the **webpack** backend (which already emits them at the entry level only). It's consumer-compatible — the only first-party reader (`get-server-action-by-id.ts`) reads the entry-level values and types `workers` as `Record<string, any>`. Net diff is **−5 lines**.

Would appreciate a review / CI run — and if any manifest snapshot fixtures hard-code the per-worker fields, happy to update them.

This is a classic Windows + OneDrive issue. The error `os error 1224` means the file is locked by another process (OneDrive sync).

## Fix 1: Move project out of OneDrive (Recommended)

OneDrive locks files during sync, which breaks Turbopack's file writing.

Move your project to:
```

C:\Projects\orvalon-web-app

```
or
```

D:\dev\orvalon-web-app

```

## Fix 2: Pause OneDrive sync temporarily

If you must keep it in OneDrive:

1. Right-click OneDrive icon in system tray
2. Click "Pause syncing" → Choose "2 hours"
3. Run `npm run dev` again
4. Resume sync after you're done

## Fix 3: Exclude `.next` folder from OneDrive

1. Open OneDrive settings
2. Go to "Sync and backup" → "Advanced settings"
3. Click "Manage backup"
4. Add `.next` folder to exclusions

Or via command line (run as admin):
```powershell
$excludePath = "$env:USERPROFILE\OneDrive\Documents\GitHub\orvalon-web-app\.next"
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive\Accounts\Personal" -Name "ExcludedFolders" -Value $excludePath -Type MultiString
```

Fix 4: Disable file indexing for .next folder

1. Right-click .next folder
2. Properties → Advanced
3. Uncheck "Allow files to have contents indexed"
4. Apply to subfolders

Fix 5: Use WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)

If you want the best experience on Windows:

```bash
wsl --install
wsl
cd ~
git clone <your-repo>
npm install
npm run dev
```

OneDrive and WSL filesystem don't conflict.

Why this happens:

· OneDrive locks files during sync
· Turbopack needs exclusive write access
· Error 1224 = "user-mapped section open"
· This is specific to Windows + OneDrive

Try Fix 1 first. moving out of OneDrive is the permanent solution. Let me know if you need more help!

This is a common issue with Turbopack and file watchers. Here's how to fix it:

## Fix 1: Increase file limit (Linux/macOS)

Check current limit:
```bash
ulimit -n
```

Increase temporarily:

```bash
ulimit -n 10000
```

Make it permanent (add to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc):

```bash
echo "ulimit -n 10000" >> ~/.zshrc
```

Fix 2: For macOS specifically

Create a file:

```bash
sudo nano /Library/LaunchDaemons/limit.maxfiles.plist
```

Add this content:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>limit.maxfiles</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>launchctl</string>
        <string>limit</string>
        <string>maxfiles</string>
        <string>100000</string>
        <string>100000</string>
    </array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
</dict>
</plist>
```

Then load it:

```bash
sudo launchctl load -w /Library/LaunchDaemons/limit.maxfiles.plist
```

Fix 3: Next.js specific

Add this to next.config.js:

```js
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    turbopack: {
      watchOptions: {
        ignored: ['**/node_modules/**', '**/.git/**']
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Fix 4: Clear cache

```bash
rm -rf .next
rm -rf node_modules/.cache
npm install
npm run dev
```

Temporary workaround

Use Webpack instead of Turbopack:

```bash
npm run dev -- --webpack
```

Try these in order. The ulimit fix usually resolves it for most users. Let me know which one works!

body:
This sounds like a real gap between the documented nonce flow and how production infrastructure may treat `Content-Security-Policy`.

The current docs flow depends on two different things:

1. the response `Content-Security-Policy` header, which the browser enforces
2. the same CSP value being present on the internal request headers so Next can parse the nonce and apply it to framework scripts

If a CDN/WAF strips `Content-Security-Policy` before the request reaches the renderer, the browser still receives the enforcing CSP, but Next loses the only place it currently knows how to read the nonce from. Since app code can read `x-nonce` but framework scripts cannot, this is not something userland can fully work around.

A configurable nonce source seems reasonable, for example:

```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    nonceHeader: 'x-nonce',
  },
}
```

or some equivalent App Router config. Next could still default to parsing `Content-Security-Policy` for backward compatibility, but fall back to the configured header when present.

A couple of constraints seem important:

- the nonce header must remain request-scoped and never cacheable
- it should probably only affect dynamic rendering paths, since nonce CSP is already incompatible with static/PPR shells
- the response CSP should still be the source of browser enforcement; the custom header would only be the framework nonce transport

This would match the docs pattern where middleware already sets both `Content-Security-Policy` and `x-nonce`, but would avoid relying on a response-only header name surviving the internal request pipeline.

body:
Good point about treating this as an internal transport header rather than trusting arbitrary user input.

If a config like `cspNonceHeader` existed, the docs should probably show middleware deleting or overwriting any incoming client-provided value before forwarding the request internally. Something like: generate nonce server-side, replace `x-nonce`, set the response CSP, and only then let the renderer read that internal header.

I also agree that a warning would help a lot. The confusing failure mode here is that app-owned inline scripts can be nonced correctly from `headers().get("x-nonce")`, while framework bootstrap scripts silently miss the nonce. A build/runtime diagnostic for "nonce CSP detected but no framework nonce resolved" would make this much easier to debug.
author: PrashantSinghUP64

body:
This is a real production gap that a few teams have hit. The short version is that Content-Security-Policy is specified as a response header, and CDN layers that correctly implement the spec strip it from the request side before it reaches your renderer. Vercel production does exactly this. The x-nonce custom header survives because it is not a restricted header name.

The practical workaround available today is to set a custom header in middleware alongside the Content-Security-Policy header, then read that custom header in your layout for any scripts you control directly.

In middleware.ts:

Set the nonce on a custom header such as x-nonce in addition to Content-Security-Policy.

In your root layout:

Read the nonce from x-nonce via headers() for your own inline scripts and the Script component.

The gap this does not solve is the framework bootstrap scripts that Next auto-injects, because those are controlled internally and only read from Content-Security-Policy. For those you would need Next itself to support a configurable header name, which is what this RFC is requesting.

Until that lands, one option is to use a hash-based CSP rather than a nonce-based one for the framework scripts specifically. You can obtain the sha256 of each framework bootstrap script from a local next build run and add those as script-src hashes in your CSP. The drawback is that you have to update the hashes after any Next upgrade. The nonce-based approach for your own scripts still works because those go through the x-nonce path.

Opening an issue in the Next.js repo with a pointer to this discussion and the Vercel support confirmation would help get this prioritized, since it is a regression relative to local dev and preview deploys.
